agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.mechanism: Drought kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.conditionality: This is an establishment-phase risk first, which is the phase a project funds and is exposed to: the measured damage falls mostly on seedlings and newly planted trees [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5], though established cabruca cocoa and its shade trees also died in the El Niño drought [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2]. Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The cocoa units are crop-specific and enter the row under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, with no measured damage, so it does not show the system is undamaged by extreme rainfall [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of rainstorm damage would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.mechanism: Accidental fire can damage trees and crops in silvopastoral and agrosilvopastoral systems, and post-fire re-establishment costs could be high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. In Senegal, fire is named among the causes of failed regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, together with grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots, climate change and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.conditionality: The literature units are statements rather than measurements: the Brazilian unit reports a cited author's comment on producer concern, and the Senegalese unit lists fire among several regeneration threats [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The literature sources are upper-middle-income Brazil and lower-middle-income Senegal [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.mechanism: Flooding and increased runoff from heavier rainfall could increase soil nutrient loss and erosion within tropical agroforestry systems, and flooding increases tree mortality in cacao agroforests, with older systems potentially more vulnerable [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.conditionality: The literature units are a tropics review reading earlier studies second-hand; the erosion statement is forward-looking and concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding, a no-damage finding for that crop [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2]. The coping ratings are practitioner judgements on technology sheets, not measured damage [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood]. Burkina Faso is low income and Kenya and India lower-middle income [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood, ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.mechanism: The IPCC assessment states that climate change affects agroforestry productivity much as it does individual perennial crops, through increased temperature or water stress, more crop pathogens, changes in pollinator abundance and changes in nutrient content [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one assessment statement that bundles several climate pressures rather than heat alone, notes limited research on tree crops, reports no measured damage, and records no country or income group [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1]. A second independent source or one measured finding of heat damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.mechanism: A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. In a newly-established silvopasture trial in the Adirondack region of New York, the authors note that heavy thinning of an even-aged stand to open the canopy for forage adds extra risk of wind blowdown to the trees left standing, describing tree productivity in silvopasture as at potential risk to this kind of damage, alongside livestock damage, though they say how much risk there is, and how management might reduce it, remains understudied [ev_climate_shock_orefice16_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The damage findings are second-hand: the hurricane result is cited, compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and names no location, and the seedling unit lists wind among several establishment-phase needs alongside trampling, herbivory, weeds and fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. Against them, the only measured unit, in shaded coffee in Chiapas, Mexico, found minimal vegetation damage from the hurricane, though the unit records its winds as mild [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]; a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]; and the Burkina Faso rating is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. Burkina Faso is low income, India lower-middle and Brazil and Mexico upper-middle income [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]. This newer finding is also an author assertion rather than a measured blowdown event, and it adds further high-income USA evidence to a row that already transfers as out of context against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_climate_shock_orefice16_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.mechanism: Across sub-practices, agroforestry trees and shrubs add habitat and species diversity relative to the land uses they replace. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system had the largest earthworm Simpson diversity index (0.62) against the smallest in sole pigeon pea (0.41) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a coffee meta-analysis found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems than conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption increased tree diversity by one to three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and a WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates both animal diversity and habitat diversity increased, noting many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Colombian silvopasture, a global meta-analysis found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with the gain largest for invertebrates (53.7%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]; a Colombian World Bank project evaluation reports increased species richness and abundance, including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], bird monitoring there found four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. For linear plantings, reviews state that windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2], that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation across fragmented tropical farm landscapes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4], and that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica report that live fences increase landscape connectivity, creating local corridors for fauna and flora, which they see as positive for native biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. A tropical agroforestry meta-analysis found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A global silvopastoral meta-analysis breaks the 28.4% biodiversity gain down further: native-tree silvopasture held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and planted-tree silvopasture held 20.9% more, with invertebrate abundance specifically about 60% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.conditionality: The roll-up reads strong because its strongest-evidenced sub-practices do: silvopastoral, shaded perennial-crop and planted silvoarable systems each read a strong gain on their own, and none of the remaining sub-practices (cross-family, linear-boundary, regeneration-based farmland, each reading only a slight gain) is large or negative enough to pull the pooled picture down or flip the direction. Set against the gains, when traditional shaded coffee/cacao agroforest is intensified to sparse-shade plantation, a global meta-analysis found total species richness fell 46% and forest-species richness fell 65%, and converting natural forest to agroforest itself cost 11% of total species richness and 35% of forest-species richness — measured harm from two independent sources, read against intensification and against standing forest rather than against open farmland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct yield-biodiversity trade-off [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The same silvopastoral meta-analysis that found a gain against open pasture also found native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower biodiversity than native forest — a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture counterfactual, so it does not contradict the open-pasture gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. A windbreak study in Queensland found the plantings useful for some birds but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, with much lower wildlife value than riparian vegetation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3], and the same pest-control meta-analysis that found more natural enemies found no significant effect of agroforestry on natural-enemy diversity in most studies (7 of 11) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. Most units describe direction without a size, and the meta-analyses behind the clearest numbers (cocoa intensification, silvopasture) do not enumerate their study countries, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. In Nicaraguan shade coffee, most certification schemes (Fairtrade, Organic+Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, Utz) raised a tree-diversity index used as a habitat-quality proxy, but one scheme, C.A.F.E. Practices, had the opposite, negative effect, showing the gain is not automatic across certification regimes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. A review of the same kind of Mexican coffee intensification gradient found species richness of ants, butterflies and birds declining as shade is simplified from forest through traditional and commercial polyculture to shaded monoculture, echoing the intensification harm already in this row [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1]. A nature-based-solutions policy review frames the biodiversity benefit as likely but conditional: it depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species planted, not a guaranteed property of agroforestry as such [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. The new Colombian dung-beetle evidence adds a fourth independent silvopastoral source and reads as a benefit, reinforcing rather than offsetting the measured harm already in this row [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.mechanism: On pastoral rangeland, trees raise biodiversity mainly by adding habitat structure and by supporting seed dispersal into the pasture. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral systems (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found biodiversity 28.4% higher in silvopasture than in open pastures; broken down by system type, silvopasture built around existing native trees held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and silvopasture with planted trees held 20.9% more, with invertebrate biodiversity specifically 53.7% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Costa Rican cattle pastures, a review of Central American silvopastoral research reports that windbreak trees support seed rain — animals visiting the trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the landscape — and cites a study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.conditionality: A related measure from the same global meta-analysis — invertebrate abundance, as distinct from the invertebrate biodiversity/richness figure above — found a large point estimate under native-tree silvopasture (+60%) that was not statistically significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10], which is part of why agreement, not strength, holds the class at moderate rather than strong. The meta-analysis is a global pooled result with no country or income-group breakdown of its own, so only the Costa Rican windbreak-seed-rain finding ties this row to a named country; Costa Rica is high income, so while the global meta-analysis evidence transfers only loosely to the LIC/LMIC target, the row as a whole transfers as adjacent rather than squarely in context [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.mechanism: A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee and cocoa reports, from a meta-analysis of 74 studies, a stronger decline in total species richness from agroforestry to plantations (−46%) than from forest to agroforestry (−11%), and, from another study, bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.conditionality: The shaded-coffee and cocoa review figures are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and the review notes the shaded systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. The harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The richness drop from forest to agroforestry (−11%) marks that shaded systems hold less than forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1]. All units are crop-specific coffee or cocoa; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries, while the review's studies are not assigned a country [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. The Kenyan WOCAT compiler rates animal and habitat diversity as increased on FMNR sites, noting that many animal species find safe habitats there and that FMNR sites provide more habitats than degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. A meta-analysis of cocoa, drawing mainly on lower-middle-income countries, found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and in Nicaraguan coffee most certification schemes had positive impacts on a tree diversity index used as a proxy for habitat quality [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The harm finding in this row is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Among the Nicaraguan schemes, C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one with a negative impact on tree diversity, and that finding is read second-hand [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The Kenyan units are compiler ratings against degraded sites rather than species surveys, and the Niger result counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. No unit gives a size for the gain in animal or habitat diversity.

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report attributes increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species, to silvopastoral systems at farm and landscape level [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], and in the Colombian Amazon piedmont silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The Colombian project evaluations give no effect sizes, and the deforestation result enters as a forest-cover component rather than a measured biodiversity outcome [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia only. The Colombian bird and ant figures are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: The carbon evidence splits by sub-practice. Silvopastoral systems read strongest on their own, planted silvoarable and regeneration-based farmland read a moderate gain, and cross-family and linear-boundary readings are only slight — so the roll-up states a moderate gain rather than the pooled slight reading. In Colombia, a World Bank project evaluation reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees, live fences and intensive silvopastoral systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10], Costa Rican silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1], and a global land-use-conversion meta-analysis found soil organic carbon rose 31 to 66% converting agriculture to silvopasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39]. In Ethiopia, FMNR-based reforestation projects audited by forestry experts sequestered 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 at two sites since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. Under regeneration-based parkland systems, soil carbon is reported 46% higher under Faidherbia albida canopy than outside it in Senegal [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1], a pan-Sahelian review of shrub and tree parklands found soil total carbon 20 to 75% higher under woody canopies than open fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2], and in Honduras, organic matter content in Quesungual fields rose from 2.4% to 4.5% over four years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates carbon and greenhouse-gas sequestration strongly increased, citing tree-cover gain through afforestation or FMNR as a way to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. For linear and cross-family plantings, a review of East African agroforestry found aboveground carbon of 26.7 Mg C/ha held in trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5], and a pan-tropical soil study found agroforestry significantly raised soil organic carbon by an overall effect size of 1.21 compared with crop monocultures, with a 40% rise in soil organic carbon, 13% in nitrogen storage and 50% lower soil erosion [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global technical mitigation potential of 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr for agroforestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence study of silvopastoral systems converted from Brachiaria pasture found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile against the traditional pasture it replaced, but did find a soil-carbon gain in the deepest sampled layer, which the authors read as showing the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil also reports that retaining native trees (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, though it gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1]. In Ghana, a plot-survey model of hybrid cocoa found that moderate shade gave a net greenhouse-gas removal increment of 127%, or 3.7 Mg CO2eq per hectare per year, over full or near-full sun hybrid cocoa [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: Almost none of this evidence is a measured net CO2e balance for the practice itself: most of it is modelled regional or global mitigation potential (IPCC, Roe et al.), a carbon stock without a time denominator, or a single-gas figure, which is why confidence stays only medium despite the growing pool of 100 units and high agreement on direction. Held against the pattern, in Niger after four years scattered Ziziphus trees raised soil carbon by 5 to 10% and nitrogen by 10 to 15%, but the differences were not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1], and in Ethiopia soil organic carbon, total nitrogen and other chemical and physical soil properties did not significantly differ under versus outside Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of one season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]. Converting existing forest to agroforestry is also measured as a loss in several readings of the same global meta-analysis — not the adoption pathway this cell is about — and the silvopastoral gains sit mostly in upper-middle-income Colombia and high-income Costa Rica, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target despite the strong Latin American silvopastoral signal [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. The Colombian Amazon system was established on tilled, limed, phosphate-treated and re-seeded pasture alongside the new trees, so the deeper-layer gain cannot be credited to the trees alone, and the full-profile result found no significant change at all, adding a null to the pool rather than strengthening the gain. This Ghanaian estimate is modelled rather than directly measured and compares two shade densities within the same cocoa system rather than agroforestry against no trees at all; the authors note the shade contrast is confounded by differences in fertiliser use and hand pollination between the plots surveyed, so it adds a lower-middle-income data point without moving the row off its existing moderate reading [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1]. The Brazilian pasture soil-carbon finding is likewise a narrative review of an underlying primary study rather than a new measurement, and adds further upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence to the row's existing adjacent transfer [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Trees on rainfed cropland add carbon to the soil, mainly under their canopies, through litter and root inputs on soils depleted by annual cropping. A meta-analysis of semi-arid West Africa found that shrubs and trees on agricultural fields raised soil total carbon by 20 to 75%, an effect ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping under the canopies of woody perennials [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil organic carbon storage [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. An FAO review for Senegal cites a meta-analysis by Sileshi (2016) that soil under the canopy of Faidherbia albida holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than soil outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. In a 10-year field experiment on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon reached 0.59% under a Gmelina–mango–pigeon pea system against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from 0.30% at the start [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. In southern Malawi, soil carbon showed a trend upward with a Tephrosia relay intercrop, 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: Not every field trial finds the gain. In Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, soil organic carbon did not significantly differ under and outside the canopy of Faidherbia albida at the end of the 2013 season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1], and in Niger, after four years, the block with Ziziphus trees held 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. What separates the results, as far as the evidence says, is time and where the carbon is measured: the large gains are under canopies or after a decade of tree growth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1], while the null results come from single seasons or a few years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Under-canopy figures do not scale to the whole field: the parkland comparisons set soil under the tree against soil outside it, so the field-level gain depends on how much of the field the canopies cover [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The evidence is soil carbon only, a component of carbon removals; it does not add up storage in tree biomass, and the West African meta-analysis reports ranges across studies rather than a pooled effect [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]. The global meta-analysis also found that converting pasture rather than cropland to agroforestry did not affect soil carbon stocks, so the gain applies to cropland conversion [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading of Sileshi (2016) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. Most of the evidence is from low- and lower-middle-income West Africa, Ethiopia, Malawi and India, within the LIC/LMIC target. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: On rangeland, trees added to grazed pasture store carbon in wood and roots and can lower nitrogen losses; Colombian intensive silvopastoral systems and Argentine silvopasture built from degraded native woodland are described as raising carbon capture [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. The soil-carbon gain is the weak part: global meta-analyses find silvopasture had the lowest increase in soil carbon of the agroforestry types, or no change at all, when converted from pasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The benefit rests on tree carbon rather than soil carbon, and on direction-only statements; no study in this row states how much carbon is gained. Expect little soil-carbon change where silvopasture replaces existing grassland, and treat the row as a slight benefit until measured stock changes are available. Against that weak soil-carbon signal, a review of semi-arid Brazilian pastures reports that retaining native trees in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture, though without a carbon value — a narrative counter-example from a single secondary-cited study, not a new measured stock change [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In tree-perennial systems (shaded coffee, cocoa and similar tree crops), carbon accumulates mainly in the aboveground biomass of the shade trees and the crop together, with soil carbon showing a more mixed picture. A pan-tropical review of cocoa agroforestry (across Ghana, Bolivia, Indonesia and other countries) found total biomass carbon (above- and below-ground, cocoa plus shade trees) on average 2.5 times higher than in cocoa monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ghana, a model of currently recommended shade-tree densities in Hybrid cocoa found a net greenhouse-gas removal increment of 127% (3.7 Mg CO2 equivalent per ha per year) over the unshaded baseline [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1]. In Costa Rica, an eight-year eddy-covariance measurement of coffee agroforestry plots (trees, coffee, litter and soil together) found mean carbon storage of 3.6 tonnes of carbon per ha per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and a review reports 29.8 Mg of carbon per ha more in the aboveground biomass of shaded coffee plots than in full-sun coffee plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. A systematic review of East African agroforestry found aboveground carbon in perennial tree-crop systems averaging 29.9 ± 12.7 Mg of carbon per ha [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4], and the same review's modelled estimates for Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee systems translate to biomass carbon of 139.5 and 153.4 Mg per ha respectively, against 96.6 Mg per ha for enset-tree alone [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. A global review of coffee agroforestry reports soil organic matter improved by 20 to 35% under shade [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The soil-carbon signal is not uniform: the same pan-tropical cocoa review that found the large biomass-carbon gain found no significant difference in soil organic carbon or total soil carbon between cocoa agroforestry and monoculture, the one exception among soil chemical properties being higher soil pH in monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1] — so the strong class rests on aboveground biomass carbon, not soil carbon. The Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee figures are modelled with the CO2FIX model and exceed the review's own regional empirical estimates, and are specific to those crops rather than the practice generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The Costa Rican eddy-covariance figure is also a measured storage figure before deducting carbon exported from the system in harvested coffee and pruned wood over the same period [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5]. The evidence spans lower-middle-income West Africa and East Africa, high-income Costa Rica, and upper-middle-income Latin American and Southeast Asian cocoa countries, so while most units sit inside the LIC/LMIC target, the class draws on some high-income evidence too.

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance of trees, coffee, litter and soil gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29.8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: These units come from high-income Costa Rica, from coffee and silvopastoral systems, and the shaded-coffee and silvopasture figures are cited secondary results [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. They lie outside the LIC/LMIC target income band and should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems without local evidence [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, trees on farms raise both biomass and soil carbon. Across sub-Saharan Africa, agroforestry improved soil organic carbon over controls (RR 1.2) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]; in West African fields, the presence of shrubs and trees raised soil total C overall, though variably (+ 20 to 75%), ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]; and a meta-analysis cited for Senegal reports 46 per cent more soil organic carbon under Faidherbia canopy than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil, with much of the above-ground carbon held in homegardens, perennial tree-crop systems and trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5]. On degraded lateritic soils in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system raised soil organic carbon to 0.59% after 10 years, against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12]. A multi-country restoration programme observed an overall relative increase of 3% in soil organic carbon over baseline and a significant association between scaling up trees on-farm and gains in soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_4]. Modelled regional potentials put agroforestry at 0.19 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Africa and the Middle East and 0.37 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Asia and the developing Pacific at up to $100/tCO2eq [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. In Ghana, a plot-survey model of hybrid cocoa found that moderate shade gave a net greenhouse-gas removal increment of 127%, or 3.7 Mg CO2eq per hectare per year, over full or near-full sun hybrid cocoa [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: On-farm measurements are mixed: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; at Sadore in Niger, soil cropped with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held 5 to 10% more soil organic carbon than soil cropped without them, but the difference was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; cocoa agroforestry showed no significant differences in soil chemical properties from monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua had positive but not statistically significant impacts on above-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. The programme's 3% gain varied significantly across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2]. Several units are stocks rather than annual rates, the Ethiopian project totals carry no per-hectare denominator, and the regional potentials are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. The pooled size rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component of sequestration [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is a compiler judgement, not a measured stock [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Coffee, cocoa, coconut and enset units are crop-specific [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kumar22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. This modelled Ghanaian estimate reinforces the LIC/LMIC reading without adding a second, independently measured net-CO2e figure: the shade contrast is confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the surveyed plots, so the row's strong reading still rests mainly on the silvopastoral and parkland gains already described above [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Across several independent global meta-analyses of soil organic carbon (SOC) under agroforestry, trees replacing cropland consistently raise SOC. A meta-analysis of paired agroforestry-versus-adjacent-cropland/pasture studies found agroforestry held soil C stocks of 126 Mg C/ha, 19% more than cropland or pasture, driven by litter from tree pruning and herbaceous root inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]. A separate paired-comparison meta-analysis found agroforestry increased SOC stocks by an average of 25.9% (95% CI 17.4–34.4%), with a greater gain when trees were established in cropland than in pasture, and converting cropland specifically to agroforestry generally increased SOC storage [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. A meta-analysis built for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock-change factor of 1.25 for cropland converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. A fourth, larger land-use-conversion meta-analysis found SOC stocks rose significantly converting agriculture to agroforestry, by 26%, 40% and 34% at different sampling depths, and from pasture/grassland to agroforestry by 9% and 10% at different depths [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_12, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_29, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_19]. By specific agroforestry type, the same meta-analysis found agriculture-to-agrisilviculture gains of 10 to 40% depending on depth, agriculture-to-agrosilvopastoral gains of 21 to 30%, and agriculture-to-silvopasture gains of 31 to 66% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_15, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_34, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_26, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_35, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: Set against these gains, converting existing forest to agroforestry instead loses SOC: the IPCC-coefficient meta-analysis found a stock-change factor of 0.89 for forest converted to agroforestry (less than the cropland factor of 1.25, indicating a loss rather than a gain) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2], and the land-use-conversion meta-analysis found forest-to-agroforestry losses of 22%, and by type, 12% for agrisilviculture and 44% for silvopasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_7]. Converting uncultivated or degraded land also sometimes lost SOC — 23% for agroforestry generally and 47% for silvopasture specifically — which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of that counterfactual category (bare land, degraded land and no-tree controls pooled together), and converting pasture to agrisilviculture lost 11%, attributed by the authors to the loss of perennial-grass root inputs once trees replace grass [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_20, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_36]. Two further independent meta-analyses agree that converting pasture specifically (rather than cropland) to agroforestry often shows no significant SOC change, because perennial pasture grass already supplies large belowground carbon inputs that dominate the soil carbon pool whether or not trees are added, and silvopasture had the smallest or no increase in soil carbon of any agroforestry type for the same reason [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. The land-use-conversion meta-analysis itself reports null results at several depths for pasture, forest-plantation and uncultivated-land conversions, and even finds no significant SOC influence from any land-use conversion to agroforestry at its deepest sampled profile [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_22, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_23, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_31, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_32, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_33, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_41]. None of these four meta-analyses lists the countries or income groups behind its pooled estimate, so the row is scoped as mixed income context rather than tied directly to the LIC/LMIC target, though the land-use-conversion study notes its base spans multiple countries across the Americas, Africa and Asia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In upper-middle-income contexts (Brazil, Colombia), the evidence for carbon gains comes mostly from large modelled national or project-level estimates alongside narrative or partial soil-carbon findings. A World Bank evaluation of a Colombian silvopastoral project modelled net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 tonnes of CO2 equivalent from converting pastureland to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. A review of Colombian intensive silvopastoral systems reports a preliminary greenhouse-gas balance in which lower nitrogen losses and higher carbon capture offset the systems' methane emissions from livestock [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. A global mitigation-potential model finds agroforestry is the highest cost-effective land-based mitigation measure of any kind in Eastern Europe and West-Central Asia (EEWA), at 0.18 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year, 24% of the region's cost-effective total [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_5]. On soil carbon specifically, a review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports total soil carbon significantly higher where native trees were left standing in pasture than in pasture without them, though without a carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1], and a Colombian Amazon study found silvopasture raised soil organic carbon stocks in the subsurface 20-30 cm layer compared with the low-productivity pasture it replaced [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A related Colombian evaluation found properties with silvopastoral interventions had significantly lower deforestation rates than untreated control properties, retaining more forest cover alongside the carbon-stock evidence, though it does not itself measure carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: None of these units states a per-hectare or per-year sequestration rate that can set a strength class: the Colombian project figure is a programme-wide total with no area or time denominator given in the passage, the regional mitigation-potential figure is a national/regional model, and the silvopastoral GHG balance and the Brazilian soil-carbon finding are narrative rather than numeric — which is why strength is recorded as not quantified in the evidence. Soil carbon is not uniformly positive even within this scope: the same Colombian Amazon study that found a subsurface gain also found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled profile when silvopasture replaced the traditional pasture it was compared with, averaged across both of its sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1]. All seven units are from upper-middle-income Brazil or Colombia, matching this scope row's own target, which is why it transfers in_context rather than merely adjacent.

agroforestry__catchment_water_yield.mechanism: Trees change how much rain reaches groundwater and streams in opposite ways. On the recharge side, the IPCC assessment states that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], and, combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, Ilstedt et al. derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. On the water-use side, a review cites Wallace et al. (2005): because agroforestry systems include a share of trees, they use more water than pure agricultural systems, though less than full-cover forest, leaving less water to feed groundwater and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. Groundwater recharge is used here as a component of catchment water yield. In a New Zealand silvopasture trial, winter moisture available to recharge the soil profile was lower under silvopasture than under open pasture (113 against 142 mm in a normal-rainfall winter), and after a wet winter, deep drainage below 2 m was detected only under open pasture, not under the silvopastures, which the authors read as the trees retaining and using most of the incoming rainfall [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].
agroforestry__catchment_water_yield.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is the balance between higher tree water use and better infiltration, which tree density sets. The recharge gains are qualified to moderate density and to an optimal intermediate density in dryland parklands, so the benefit does not keep rising with tree cover [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]; the loss rests on the general point that more trees transpire more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. The recharge statements are about drylands, while the water-use statement is general, so the row cannot say which side wins in a given catchment. All units are second-hand readings in reviews or assessments, the recharge units rest on the same primary work by Ilstedt et al., none states a size or a country, and no unit measures water leaving a catchment or reaching downstream users [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6, ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. This measured New Zealand evidence strengthens the loss side of the row directly, rather than only the general point that more trees transpire more water: both readings are from the same single silvopasture experiment, high-income temperate evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target, so the row's low agreement and out-of-context transfer are unchanged [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].

agroforestry__cost_per_beneficiary.mechanism: A programme cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices cost $66 per household in Ghana, where the practice was farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR), and $201 per household in Rwanda, where it was tree-planting agroforestry [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. The denominator is each household adopting at least one land restoration practice [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3].
agroforestry__cost_per_beneficiary.conditionality: The two figures are arms of one programme with different practices and countries (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income), inside the LIC/LMIC target, and the source links the lower Ghana cost to FMNR versus tree planting where household land is more limited [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. They are programme expenditure levels, not cost changes against a control, and with one source and two arms they do not pool into a range [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

agroforestry__cost_per_hectare_restored.mechanism: The same programme reports $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana and $1,387 per hectare for tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda, counted per hectare where at least one land restoration practice is adopted [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. In the United States, establishing silvopasture from forest in a research trial required an initial timber-harvesting (thinning) cost of $1,059 per hectare, plus $167.04 per hectare for forage seeding and $185.33 per hectare for fencing and water infrastructure [ev_project_cost_orefice16_1, ev_project_cost_orefice16_2, ev_project_cost_orefice16_3].
agroforestry__cost_per_hectare_restored.conditionality: The two figures are arms of one programme that differ widely by practice and country (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income), so they describe two different costs rather than one pooled range [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. They are programme expenditure levels, not costs relative to a control [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. These US figures are a different cost basis again from the Ghanaian and Rwandan programme-expenditure figures already in this row: they are actual trial costs for specific establishment line items on one research site, the timber-harvest cost applied equally to the open-pasture comparator rather than being specific to silvopasture, and the US is high income against lower-middle-income Ghana and low-income Rwanda, so none of the figures in this row can be pooled into one range [ev_project_cost_orefice16_1, ev_project_cost_orefice16_2].

agroforestry__cost_per_tco2e_avoided.mechanism: The IPCC land report states that the cost of agroforestry as a response option is less than 10 USD per tonne CO2e, among the lower-cost options, against as much as 250 USD for BECCS [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4].
agroforestry__cost_per_tco2e_avoided.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class for this cell: it is one global upper-bound statement citing an earlier assessment, with no country, income group, currency year or practice detail, and the source adds that economic barriers other than cost may prevent implementation [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4]. A second independent source or one measured cost per tonne from a project would let the cell state a class.

agroforestry__cost_reduction.mechanism: Trees change farm costs in both directions, mostly through labour. Some systems save cost: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, an estimate from a Bank-commissioned business case attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. Others add cost: in the forest zone of Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 (38%) person-days per hectare per year and variable costs by 34% averaged over the trial, for hedgerow planting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]; and at Ibadan, Nigeria, maize mulched with cut-and-carry tree leaves needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, with 96% of the labour going to collecting and managing the mulch and only 4% to weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model adds two further labour-cost readings, both increases: annual labour for maize production under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is reported increased by 53 percent against the traditional bush-fallow control, because of the added labour for hedgerow pruning, and under the closer 2 m spacing the model assumes total labour increases by 87 percent, since more hedgerows need pruning [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6].
agroforestry__cost_reduction.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is where the trees' labour falls. Where the trees grow in the field and suppress weeds, as the Rwandan Tephrosia did, weeding labour falls [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]; where tree biomass must be pruned, cut and carried, the extra handling outweighs the weeding saved, and in Nigeria the mulch was grown on a separate plot and carried in [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Between them sit no-change findings: A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies in low- and middle-income countries reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952), with an interval spanning a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), pooling agroforestry applied alone or in bundles [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The Cameroon costs mix establishment and recurrent pruning labour, and its trees were pruned only from the second year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Colombian figure is a modelled recurrent saving from an upper-middle-income country and does not pool with the relative changes [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. The coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. The field evidence is otherwise from low-income Rwanda and lower-middle-income Cameroon and Nigeria, within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1, ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both readings add to the cost-increase side of this row rather than the cost-saving side: like the Cameroon and Nigeria mulching evidence already here, the extra labour is pruning and handling tree biomass, not time saved on weeding. The 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier cited labour study rather than measured by the modelling authors themselves, and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption (more hedgerows to prune at closer spacing), not a measurement. Both are lower-middle-income Nigerian evidence, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.mechanism: Trees in rainfed cropland raise labour costs rather than lowering them. In Cameroon, averaged over 3 years and taking the traditional maize/groundnut system as the reference, planting Leucaena hedgerows raised variable costs by 34%, and labour rose from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare per year, for hedgerow establishment, cutting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In south-western Nigeria, maize mulched with leaves cut and carried from multipurpose trees needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, and with Gliricidia sepium or Senna siamea mulch 96% of the total labour went on collecting and managing the mulch [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.conditionality: Both units are research-managed trials in the sub-humid and humid tropics of West and Central Africa, lower-middle-income settings. The higher costs bought higher returns in Cameroon, where unfertilised alley cropping gave the highest net benefit, so cost here is not the same as net loss [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Where labour or land is scarce, the extra labour can make the practice unattractive [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].

agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.mechanism: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.conditionality: The evidence is thin, so confidence is low and no cost class is set. The Rwandan saving is a labour figure from a small on-farm trial, and Tephrosia there is a cut-back mulch shrub rather than a shade tree, so it says little about the cost of shade-tree systems [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. The cocoa meta-analysis finds no cost difference, and its costs are annual production costs that in some studies include certification or land rent [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. Both units are crop-specific (coffee or cocoa) and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; the evidence is from low- and lower-middle-income producers.

agroforestry__cost_reduction__income_gro.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, the evidence finds agroforestry costs sometimes lower, sometimes higher and sometimes unchanged, depending on what the trees do to the farm's labour. Where the trees replace a task, labour falls: in Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia intercropping required 30 man-days per hectare less than current farmer management because less weeding was needed [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. Where the trees add a task, labour rises: in Nigerian maize, plots mulched with tree prunings needed more labour than the fertilizer and untreated controls, with 96% of the labour spent collecting and managing mulch and only 4% weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]; and in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%) and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Pooled studies sit between: a meta-analysis of field studies reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952) [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1], and a cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__income_gro.conditionality: The studies disagree, so no direction is stated. What separates them is the labour the trees bring: the saving comes with a weed-suppressing intercrop in an established tree crop [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3], while the cost rises come with cut-and-carry mulching and hedgerow pruning in annual maize systems, where cutting, carrying and spreading prunings is the added work [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and fell from the first to the third year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The pooled meta-analysis interval spans both a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), its table pools observations where agroforestry was applied alone or in bundles with other practices, and the costs are mostly variable rather than establishment costs [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The cocoa unit is crop-specific and draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. For a project, labour demand at planting and pruning, and whether it falls in seasonal peaks, is the cost question to check.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: One tropics review, citing earlier studies, reports that severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3], and that another study found drought exposure did not increase seedling mortality, despite impaired growth [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: both units come from one review reading other studies second-hand, they point in different directions, and none is a measured finding of the review itself; no country or income group is recorded [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. A second independent source or one measured finding of drought damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: A systematic review reports, second-hand, a hypothetical study in Hawaii finding that the flammability of tropical agroforestry systems is likely not to be affected by increasing temperatures (+2°C) [ev_fire_hazard_watts22_15].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one modelled statement from a high-income US setting outside the LIC/LMIC target, and it concerns how warming changes flammability, not how much damage fire does to trees when it occurs [ev_fire_hazard_watts22_15]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: One tropics review, citing earlier studies, states that flooding and increased runoff from heavier rainfall could increase soil nutrient loss and erosion within tropical agroforestry systems [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single forward-looking statement read second-hand, it concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and no country or income group is recorded [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13]. A second independent source or one measured finding of flood damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: Climate change affects agroforestry productivity much as it does individual perennial crops, through increased temperature or water stress, more crop pathogens, changes in pollinator abundance and changes in nutrient content [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: This IPCC assessment statement covers several climate pressures at once, not heat alone, and notes there is little research on tree crops [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1]. It is global, with no country or income group recorded [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one study read second-hand, it compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and the citing passage names no location [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind or cyclone damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__biodiversity.mechanism: Across sub-practices pooled together, agroforestry trees and shrubs are reported to add habitat and pest-control value. A tropical-agroforestry review states that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation, and that retaining or establishing trees in agricultural land may be a critical component of conservation efforts in fragmented landscapes, with floristic diversity that can be high and a substantial number of animal species able to exploit these habitats for feeding, movement and, in some cases, reproduction [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. A meta-analysis of tropical agroforestry studies found natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls, as part of a general benefit to natural pest control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A separate perspective review states that agroforestry is likely to have biodiversity benefits compared to conventional arable, pasture or forestry, though this depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].
agroforestry__cross_family__biodiversity.conditionality: The same meta-analysis that found more natural enemies also reports, for the diversity (rather than abundance) of natural enemies, that most studies (7 of 11) showed no effect and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect and the rest split evenly between positive and negative — held out here as a finding on a narrower measure of the same taxon group, not a contradiction of the abundance result [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. The review-level units generalise across cited studies rather than measuring anything themselves, and the review qualifies that agroforestry elements 'are not substitutes for the original vegetation' and that almost all its cited studies were in landscapes with some remnant forest nearby, so element value and landscape context are confounded [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. None of the four units names a country, income group or farming system for this pooled row, so although the pattern is consistent it only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].

agroforestry__cross_family__carbon_seque.mechanism: Pooled across sub-practices, modelled mitigation-potential and stock-comparison studies consistently find a carbon benefit, though almost none of them gives a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. A pan-tropical soil study (71 studies, 225 pairs) found agroforestry significantly increased soil organic carbon storage compared with crop monocultures (overall effect size 1.21) and reduced soil erosion by 50%, with soil organic carbon up 40%, nitrogen storage up 13%, available nitrogen up 46% and available phosphorus up 11% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global analysis estimating agroforestry's technical mitigation potential at 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr, and further estimates a technical potential of 4.1 (0.3–9.4) GtCO2eq/yr for 2020-2050, of which 0.8 (0.4–1.1) GtCO2eq/yr is available at USD100/tCO2 [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5]. A regional modelling study finds agroforestry's mitigation density about 45 tCO2eq/ha, and across the Africa-Middle East region its cost-effective mitigation potential at 0.19 GtCO2eq/yr (8% of the regional total) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. In Brazil, a review reports agroforestry carbon sequestration rates varying by climate from 954 to 3670 tCO2/km2/yr, with a technical potential of 0.1 to 5.7 GtCO2eq/yr, the largest among the land uses it compared [ev_carbon_sequestration_santos25_3]. One directly measured finding in the row combines biomass and soil carbon sequestration with changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions and estimates a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 t CO2eq/ha/yr, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline survey found a relative 3% increase in soil organic carbon compared with baseline, with significant variation across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2].
agroforestry__cross_family__carbon_seque.conditionality: Only one of these 67 units — the biomass-plus-soil-plus-gas estimate above — is a measured net balance for the practice itself; the rest are modelled regional or global mitigation potentials, single-gas or stock-only figures, or review restatements of other studies, so the engine cannot let most of them set the class, which is why confidence stays very low despite the consistent direction. A further eight units are held out because their comparator is existing natural forest, not the farming system the practice would actually replace: converting forest to agroforestry lost soil organic carbon in every reading — 22 to 26% at shallow depth and 24% for agrisilviculture specifically — and forest-to-silvopastoral/agrosilvopastoral conversions likewise lost 27 to 36% at various depths, reversals that describe deforestation for agroforestry, not the cropland- or pasture-to-agroforestry adoption pathway this cell is about [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_14, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_25, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_37]. None of the global modelling or meta-analysis units names the countries behind its pooled estimate, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target rather than being confidently in context [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__catchment_wa.mechanism: Trees both add and use water in a catchment, and the evidence here shows each pathway once. The IPCC assessment states, citing earlier studies (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020), that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density; recharge is read here as a component of catchment water yield [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1]. A review of agroforestry water and soil losses states, citing Wallace et al. (2005), that because agroforestry systems include a proportion of trees they use more water than pure agricultural systems (though less than a full-cover forest), leaving less water to feed groundwater bodies and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__catchment_wa.conditionality: The sources point in opposite directions, so the row states no direction. What separates them, as far as the evidence says, is tree density and the balance between tree water use and the water trees let into the soil: the recharge gain is qualified to moderate density in drylands [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], while the loss is the general case of trees using more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. Both are second-hand statements in syntheses (the IPCC chapter and a literature review), neither carries a size, a country or a measured catchment outcome, so the cell cannot say how large either effect is. A measured water-yield or recharge comparison of agroforestry against cropland in an LIC/LMIC catchment would resolve it; tree density and species water use are the design questions for water-scarce catchments.

agroforestry__cross_family__cost_per_tco.mechanism: The IPCC land report states that the cost of agroforestry as a response option is less than 10 USD per tonne CO2e, among the lower-cost options, against as much as 250 USD for BECCS [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__cost_per_tco.conditionality: This is one global upper-bound statement citing an earlier assessment, with no country, income group, currency year or practice detail, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked and the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4]. The source adds that economic barriers other than cost may prevent implementation [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4].

agroforestry__cross_family__cost_reducti.mechanism: A meta-analysis of agroforestry against a control reports a log response ratio of production cost per hectare of -0.014 (-1.39%) across 10 studies and 10 sites, close to no change in cost [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__cost_reducti.conditionality: The result is not significant (p = 0.952) and its interval runs from -29.06 to 68.32%, so it does not demonstrate a cost reduction, and it gives no cost amount [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. It is a single relative measure tagged LIC/LMIC without listed countries [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__drought__agr.mechanism: Trees raise the soil water available to crops: a sub-Saharan African meta-analysis found agroforestry raised soil moisture over controls (RR 1.6) and raised infiltration even more, and a cited synthesis reports perennial trees added to cropland raise rainfall infiltration by 59% [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10]. A review also reports that understorey crop yield under drought can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13].
agroforestry__cross_family__drought__agr.conditionality: The quantified evidence is soil moisture and infiltration, used as a component proxy for drought impact rather than a measured drought outcome [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10].
