The infiltration and yield statements are review-level citations, and the same review notes shade can reduce understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1].

A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with an even split of gains and losses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13].

agroforestry__cross_family__rural_povert.mechanism: An East African systematic review counts income among the main livelihood benefits of agroforestry, diversifying rural livelihoods and acting as a safety net in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_household_income_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report favourable financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of sub-Saharan adoption studies, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, found agroforestry adoption raises household income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001), from diversified revenue in fruit, timber and fuelwood [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, cash-crop revenues, especially from cardamom, and total income were significantly higher on farms using improved agroforestry, and gross income per capita was US$ 157 against US$ 74 on traditional farms [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In West Java, Indonesia, agroforestry had a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than swidden cultivation, according to a review's reading of Rahman et al. (2017) [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].
agroforestry__cross_family__rural_povert.conditionality: Several units show no effect or a loss: the pooled systematic-review income effect is not statistically significant, Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged and no short-term income change detectable, and some Brazilian system components were loss-making [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. The working paper's revenue measure is gross revenue, not profit, and not significant [ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Mozambique result is a review citation without an effect size [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The sub-Saharan pooled income effect rests on adopter versus non-adopter contrasts, many with weak causal identification, and its pool includes payments for ecosystem services in Mozambique, so part of that gain is a cash transfer rather than a production effect [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is gross income from a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, and the authors note household overhead costs were also higher [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. The Indonesian result is second-hand, from a small sample, and compares against swidden cultivation rather than permanent cropland [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].

agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, IPCC assessments describe agroforestry limiting erosion and stabilising soils with perennial vegetation, and farmland with agroforestry is reported more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20–50% decrease in runoff, used here as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.conditionality: The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias, and Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3]. The IPCC statements are assessment-level, and several units are review statements without effect sizes [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5, ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_12, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control, with a weighted response ratio of 1.6 for soil moisture across 62 observations from 27 studies, and 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1 [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. Wetter soil under trees eases the crop's water stress. A cited statement adds that rainfall over agricultural land can shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.conditionality: The meta-analysis pools agroforestry practices without separating soil depth, so it cannot show whether trees and crops compete for deeper water; the Faidherbia parkland evidence that does show subsoil depletion sits in the regeneration-farmland row [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The effect on infiltration was greater than that on soil moisture [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect from a secondary citation, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Groundwater-recharge findings are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows.

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: Trees cut both ways in storms. A smallholder agroforestry review notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. A Latin American adaptation review gives planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The sides differ in what is exposed: the protective statement concerns sheltering and rebuilding on the farm, while the harmful example concerns trees falling on or damaging existing infrastructure [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. Placement relative to buildings and infrastructure is therefore the design point the evidence implies. Neither unit is a measured effect on livelihoods or crops: one is a typology example and the other a narrative review statement, and neither records a country or income group, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a rainfed cropping system; the evidence is applied to rainfed cropping systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a mixed crop-livestock system; the evidence is applied to mixed crop-livestock systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a pastoral rangeland system; the evidence is applied to pastoral rangeland systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a tree-perennial system; the evidence is applied to tree-perennial systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.mechanism: Trees and live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: trees were the main source of animal feed and milk production for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Zambian, US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems, and the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]; the understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size, and few units say how large the drought benefit is [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. No unit in this row measures the benefit in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.mechanism: A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row resting on two second-hand statements that point in opposite directions, so no clear effect can be drawn [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The silvopasture statement does not mention drought, and the shelterbelt finding concerns crop yield rather than an agro-pastoral outcome, applied here by default; neither transfers directly to LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral systems [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].

agroforestry__drought__all.mechanism: Most of the evidence finds that agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the finding splits by sub-practice and some measured results show no benefit or harm. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, and trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].
agroforestry__drought__all.conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as clear benefits, the linear-boundary and cross-family cells as small benefits, and the shaded perennial-crop cell is conflicting. Few of the benefit units say how large the effect is, which also holds the class at moderate. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way: tree–maize competition for soil water in Kenya can lead to crop failure, and a Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Argentine multi-site study is the clearest statement of why severity matters: it explicitly frames the switch from facilitation to competition as a function of drought intensity, and shows the sign of the effect also depends on site aridity and on whether the stocking system is native-forest or planted silvopastoral, so it cannot be read as a single transferable number [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. The French walnut-pea result is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: agroforestry pea yield remained below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes, and the smaller drought-specific loss is a relative measure against each system's own rainfed baseline, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. Both of these are upper-middle-income Argentina and high-income France, sitting at a different distance from the LIC/LMIC target than the Kenyan and Ethiopian evidence already in this row.

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In an induced-drought experiment in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping agroforestry system, crop losses occurred only in the monocropping system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, though alley-cropped pea still yielded less overall than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row: all units come from Canada, Germany, the USA or temperate settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, which also notes N-fixation declined in both systems, the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions, and the US unit is a background statement that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. No unit says how large the effect is, and none measures it in a severe or extreme drought. The French result adds a fourth high-income unit to this scope row: a single season and site, drought imposed experimentally with rainout shelters, and the two conditions not randomised within the parcel; the benefit is a smaller drought-specific loss, not a yield advantage over full sun [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, a household survey and interviews conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought: households listed agroforestry as important for their livelihood during drought, in Burat households practising it mostly said droughts were less frequent while most households without it said the opposite, 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind, and farmers explained that deep roots let trees get water from deep down so they keep producing fruit when there is no rain [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also act as a fodder and cash reserve: in southern Zambia trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production during drought, in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet before the rains, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods while many farmers sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme stakeholders rated 14 of 22 cases as having a substantial or high effect on drought vulnerability, naming income from commercial agroforestry as one route that reduced vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression, and in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: Tree–crop competition can reverse the effect: a review cites Kenyan trials in which competition with Grevillea robusta for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and could lead to crop failure, an FAO review for Senegal finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought (some studies report higher yields near hedges in drier years, others harm to non-irrigated crops), and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. In Kinna, drought perceptions did not differ between households with and without agroforestry [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5], and the severe-drought evidence is a cited Honduran observation with no measured size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan resilience findings come from a single survey and are perception-based, the Zambian, Senegalese and competition findings are secondary citations in reviews, the Ethiopian rating credits a bundled programme rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In the Ghana cocoa experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline, and the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; both are among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline, and the cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific, entering because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.mechanism: Agroforestry raised soil moisture over controls (RR 1.6) in a sub-Saharan African meta-analysis, and a cited synthesis reports perennial trees added to cropland raise rainfall infiltration by 59% [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10]. Live fences supply fodder in the dry season when pasture is scarce, and shaded understorey crops can yield more than open systems under drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Ethiopia, income growth through commercial agroforestry is named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.conditionality: The quantified evidence is soil water, a component proxy for drought impact; the Ethiopian result is for a bundled land-management programme based on stakeholder responses, and the other units are reviews citing other studies [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. Only the Ethiopian unit names a country (low income); the rest are regional or pantropical reviews [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, even though alley-cropped yield stayed below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual farmers reported no total maize loss in the 1997 El Niño dry period, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Boundary plantings read as a small, unquantified benefit: a live-fence fodder role in drought, set against a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result sits outside the voting sub-practices, and that benefit reverses under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. This French result belongs to the planted-silvoarable cluster already described as pairing gains with a reversal: it is a cushioned loss relative to the system's own rainfed baseline, not a yield advantage over full sun, from a single season and site, and is high-income evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: Both units point to a benefit, but neither says how large it is, and neither measures a severe or extreme drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. This is a high-income temperate scope row (Canada, Germany) outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, and the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. This is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: alley-cropped pea still yielded less than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel, and is high-income temperate evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: The evidence for rainfed cropping points both ways. A review cites Kenyan trials in which maize grown with Grevillea robusta competed with the trees for limited soil water, which delayed maize flowering and development and could lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Against this, the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme income growth through commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: An FAO review for Senegal reports no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought: some studies find higher yields near hedges in drier years, while others judge the hedges could harm non-irrigated crops; and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. Whether trees help or hurt the crop in drought turns on how strongly they compete for limited soil water [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Much of the pool is second-hand: the competition result and both review findings are secondary citations, the Ethiopian rating belongs to a bundled programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation and agroforestry) rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the source of the Nigerian model notes its weak fit may understate impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock settings the evidence points the same way, though few units say how large the effect is, so the class is a slight reduction in drought impact. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Brazilian semi-arid, agroforestry biomass productivity varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, which the source attributes mainly to water availability, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species carry livestock through dry periods with high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.conditionality: The Kenyan household units are a single study of survey and farmer-interview evidence, and the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. No unit measures the effect in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: On pastoral land the benefit runs through fodder and herd condition. Live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species are used to feed livestock in the dry season and supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In Colombia, a review citing Altieri and Nicholls 2013 reports that forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011) [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. A multi-site Argentine study adds further detail on pastoral drought: forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The evidence base is thin and mostly second-hand: the silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume, the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Only the Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland systems; the live-fence review, the understorey statement and the Kenyan FMNR rating are applied here by default [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, when tree shade could decrease understorey yields [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Colombian sources are upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The same Argentine study is also the clearest statement of why the benefit is not unconditional: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years, the authors attributing the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. This is upper-middle-income Argentine evidence, consistent with the row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The units point in opposite directions and neither measures drought losses in a pastoral system: the shelterbelt result is a temperate cropping finding applied to pastoral rangeland by default, and the Costa Rican result is dry-season liveweight gain [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Both are earlier findings cited second-hand, from high-income or temperate settings outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: Against those benefits, a model-based assessment cited in a tropical agroforestry review (Onyekuru and Marchant) found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues in Nigeria under a simulated climate 1◦C warmer with 7% less annual rainfall; it enters as an income proxy and is the no-benefit result that discounts the class [ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran observation repeats Welchez and Cherrett, cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. None of the units records a pastoral or rangeland farming system: the Honduran unit concerns crops and the others name no system, so they are applied to rangeland by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. All units are from lower-middle-income countries (Honduras, Kenya, Nigeria), inside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1], and milk production in the El Niño year with the lowest rainfall in several decades still rose 10% on the previous year after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also let irrigation be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The same Argentine study is the source of this row's measured harm: it found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites — at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years, which the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The Colombian units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. All units in this scope row are upper-middle income (Argentina, Colombia), which is why it transfers in_context to its own scope.

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.mechanism: Under drought, trees in tree-crop systems have been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin) and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]; and a review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. General agroforestry reports point the same way: live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms (Blaser et al.), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; the field study by Abdulai et al. in Ghana measured this directly: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 against 170 in full sun (grams per square centimetre per day), sap flux recovered to 163 in full sun but only 37 under A. toxicaria, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses are attributed to that competition, measured in the Ghanaian shade-tree study (Abdulai et al.) as lower soil water under the shade trees than in full sun, while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia), a shade-management setting (canopy openness) or a drought year in which shade relieved the understorey [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A second separator is what is measured: the Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment found the overall better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought, so a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions for drought-exposed tree-crop systems. On the benefit side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade trees strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1], and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the harm side, a field study in Ghana found that during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to stronger competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

In a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment on cocoa, the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it; the shade there came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, that trees were the most important source of animal food and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought (Chibinga et al. 2012), that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce, and that agroforestry biomass production varied less over 4 years than conventional systems in semi-arid Brazil, attributed mainly to water availability (Martins et al. 2013) [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield was relatively improved by 12 to 20% against its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought_hazard.conditionality: Effects are not uniform, and for some adopters the trees made drought losses worse. Few units give a size, so the class is slight. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household and fodder evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya and low-income Zambia, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The French result is a relative cushioning of the drought impact, not a stated yield advantage over full sun, from a single season and site, and it is high-income evidence, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought_hazard__income_gro.mechanism: In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. agroforestry__drought_hazard__income_gro.conditionality: Both units are high-income, temperate evidence (France, Canada), outside the LIC/LMIC target, from a single season or trial each, and neither states a size for the benefit; the French result is a smaller drought-specific loss relative to the system's own rainfed baseline, not a yield advantage over full sun, and the Canadian result is reported second-hand through an IPCC assessment chapter [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3, ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4].

agroforestry__establishment_cost.conditionality: These are programme expenditures per adopting household or per adopted hectare, two denominators that cannot be pooled, from two arms of one programme (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income) [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_3, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. The quote does not identify them as establishment costs specifically, and they are levels rather than costs relative to a control [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_3, ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__fire__agro_pastoral.mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. A land-use overlay of burnt areas across six European Mediterranean countries found that, corrected for the extent of each land use, agroforestry occupied 12% of the area but was associated with only 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40%; agroforestry's share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Before that correction, the average share of fire incidents was lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
agroforestry__fire__agro_pastoral.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state rather than the farming-system counterfactual this cell asks about. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8], and the Mediterranean overlay compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland, not with the cropland or open pasture a project would convert [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6], and in the Mediterranean data grassland, not agroforestry, had the lowest unadjusted share of fires [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. The Mediterranean result that does favour agroforestry is the one against shrubland; against forest and grassland the difference was not significant [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Both studies come from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; in the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of agroforestry against the treeless farmland or pasture it replaces, ideally in an LIC/LMIC system. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is carried but cannot set the class either: it is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. It concerns natural regeneration rather than silvopasture, but its direction agrees with the comparator argument above: added tree cover adds fuel, and the compiler recommends fire breaks for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].

agroforestry__flood__agro_pastoral.mechanism: In Vietnam, an extreme flood from heavy rainfall caused 40% yield loss of regional crops, while farms with trees were less affected; the quote does not say why [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11].
agroforestry__flood__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The 40% is the regional crop loss, not the agroforestry effect, and the result is one study cited second-hand in a review [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. The evidence is from Vietnam (lower-middle income), within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11].

In Nyando District, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods, and some had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when other crops were underwater or washed away [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The same review also reports, citing Eychène et al. 2014, that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].

agroforestry__food_insecurity.mechanism: Across contexts, agroforestry raises household food security mainly through tree products adding to diets and smoothing shortfalls. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had food crop value 35% higher than non-adopters, driving greater food security [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8]. In Kenya, agrosilvopastoral extension advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 points and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Zambia, improved fallows raised the number of months per year with enough grown food by 1.069 months [ev_food_security_castle21s_3]. Across the Regreening Africa endline survey (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia), the share of respondents meeting the minimum-dietary-diversity cut-off rose from 16 to 21%, a 31% relative increase, and households that intensified tree-product use saw significant dietary-diversity gains in Ethiopia, Ghana, Niger, Rwanda and Senegal [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Kenya, fruit from on-farm trees was some farmers' only steady food source during the floods, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1].
agroforestry__food_insecurity.conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology, with increasing tree density associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands even as it raised food security in Congo Nile — measured harm for some households [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. Several units find no effect: Kenyan improved fallow showed no significant nutritional results [ev_food_security_castle21s_2], the Regreening Africa endline's food-insecurity-experience-scale score showed no substantial change [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9], Nigerien FMNR did not reduce months of perceived food shortage though it raised crop diversity [ev_food_security_haglund11_1], and the Sahel food-consumption-score gains were not statistically significant under the authors' own convention, though the authors describe them as increases [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Talensi and Nepali/Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after project self-evaluations or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the World Vision multi-country brief and the Nguyen review both note their findings cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities or, in the review's case, were guaranteed by its own inclusion rule (only studies already showing a food-security improvement were selected) [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. Most units describe direction without a size; where sizes are given (Malawi, Regreening Africa), the gains sit in low and lower-middle-income African and South Asian contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1].

agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.mechanism: Across mixed crop–livestock systems, agroforestry raises food security through added food sources and income. In Nepal, the share of households that were food-sufficient rose from 146 of 279 (52%) before a market-oriented agroforestry intervention to 192 of 279 (69%) after, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Tanzania, improved agroforestry was securing enough food throughout the year for 40% of households, against 18% of households on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level farmer-managed natural regeneration raised the household food consumption score by about 12% across Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Kenya, during floods, some farmers reported fruit from their on-farm trees as their only steady source of food while other crops were underwater or washed away, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies (such as consuming seed stock or selling oxen) during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed than a control group [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1].
agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology: increasing tree density was associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands, even as it raised the probability of food security in Congo Nile — the practice worsening the outcome for some households, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Sahelian gain from low to continuous FMNR showed no significant food-consumption-score gain in any country, and a separate measure, months with a household food deficit, found no significant effect for any FMNR intensity, though the authors read the communities as more resilient during food shortages as an inference rather than a measured result [ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African and South Asian mixed crop–livestock systems, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1].

agroforestry__frost__mixed_crop_livestoc.conditionality: The cell rests on microclimate evidence (night-time canopy temperature and radiation), a component of frost impact, rather than measured frost losses on farms [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5]. Brazilian units (upper-middle income) and a review statement has no recorded country or income group; none is from an LIC/LMIC setting, and the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3]. All three are reviews or authors citing earlier work, and none records a farming system, so the evidence is applied to each farming system by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5].
