agroforestry__gender_inequity.mechanism: A gender review finds agroforestry can offer substantial benefits to women, but their participation is low in enterprises considered men's domain such as timber and in the area and number of trees they commit [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1]. It reports, second-hand, that management labour often falls on women (in 89% of Embu households using calliandra fodder, females managed it) [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2], that 32% of males and 23% of females planted improved fallows in four Zambian villages [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3], and that in farmer-managed trials women had somewhat higher Sesbania survival than men [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further, more recent Sahelian observation: in Niger's re-greened farmer-managed natural regeneration zones, the increase in on-farm trees has, in many cases, sharply cut the time women spend collecting firewood for the household, from an average of 2.5 hours a day twenty years ago to 0.5 hour a day now [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].
agroforestry__gender_inequity.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: every unit comes from a single narrative review of sub-Saharan African studies, read second-hand, with no measured finding of its own [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. That is a before/after regional account with no control, and it adds a case where the gender effect runs the other way from the labour-burden units above, towards less time on a task that falls mainly to women, rather than confirming them [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].

agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.mechanism: In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside, and access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Senegal Ferlo and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems; the rest are general reviews applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. All units report cooling or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact, and all are reviews or assessments citing earlier studies, the Ferlo temperatures repeating Akpo et al. [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all.mechanism: Trees cool the air and soil that crops and livestock experience, through shade and altered radiation and humidity. In Ethiopia, air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under Faidherbia albida canopy compared with the open field, reaching a maximum of 29°C under the canopy against 36°C in the open, and temperature stayed above 28°C for about six hours a day in the open field against under two hours under the canopy; the authors link this cooling to reduced heat stress at the wheat's critical reproductive stages, and a crop model found that the resulting temperature reduction has a positive impact on wheat yield once nitrogen is applied [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3]. In India, a reduction in heat load under Populus deltoides agri-silviculture is linked to a 6.8% increase in wheat grain yield [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In Germany, poplar alley cropping measured 3.4°C lower air temperature than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found summer air temperature significantly reduced by 4.01% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees reduce the maximum daily temperature by an average of 1 to 2.5°C, with stronger effects on hotter, drier days, and under Acacia tortilis canopy in Senegal's Ferlo, air temperatures ranged from 29 to 36°C against 26 to 42°C outside the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. For livestock, the cooling under trees is reported to reduce heat stress directly and raise milk and weight gain: temperature under tree crowns in tropical pastures is 2 to 9°C lower than in open areas, with tree groups giving the largest reduction (3.6°C) and live fences the smallest (1.7°C) [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Milk production rose 29% under high tree-density pasture compared with low tree cover, attributed to reduced heat stress, and other work found increases above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. In Brazil's Caatinga, the black-globe temperature-humidity index fell comparing shade under tree strips with sun exposure, and strips with the most woody cover were more efficient at mitigating cattle heat load than an almost treeless system [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In Brazilian silvopasture compared with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100% [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A Peru/Colombia systematic review reports silvopastoral systems reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13°C on the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. In Senegal, access to cool zones under trees is reported to reduce livestock heat stress and so raise animal productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all.conditionality: Against this, one measured unit in Senegal finds windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots rather than cooling them, with variable impacts depending on crop and growth stage — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, which the engine counts as measured harm and discounts the class for [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter adds that while shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee, the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The Ethiopian cooling only translated to a yield response once nitrogen was applied: without applied nitrogen, simulated wheat yield did not respond to the temperature reduction under F. albida shade at all [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. No unit in this row measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot-season or hot-day conditions [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The class stays low (a slight reduction) rather than higher because most units describe temperature buffering as a component of heat stress rather than a direct livelihood outcome, several are reviews restating other studies without a size, and the Latin American livestock figures mostly come from narrative reviews in regional veterinary journals rather than controlled trials [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. The pooled evidence spans West Africa, East Africa, Latin America, South and East Asia and temperate Europe at every income level, so it transfers only as adjacent rather than squarely in context [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: On hot summer days, a poplar alley-cropping system in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than a sole wheat system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture, and cited studies found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than for cows in full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C against full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units come from Germany or Costa Rica, recorded as high income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; all but the coffee measurement are earlier studies cited in reviews [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. The coffee unit is crop-specific and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. They report air temperature or milk yield rather than measured heat-stress losses, live fences gave the smallest cooling of the arrangements compared, and the milk gain is not separated from other effects of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: In Ethiopia, Faidherbia albida trees cut the radiation reaching the wheat canopy and made the wheat 6°C cooler than open wheat [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5]. In the Ferlo, Senegal, air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged less widely than outside the canopy, and in Kenya shade trees are described as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations and can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal pull the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots with impacts that depend on the crop and its growth stage, so the evidence pools opposite signs [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. All four units are from LIC/LMIC countries (Ethiopia, Kenya, Senegal), but all are reported second-hand from earlier studies and rest on temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In Cuba, live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units are reviews citing earlier studies, and they report animal comfort rather than measured production losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.mechanism: Reviews report that tree shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Shade from live fences is reported to reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.conditionality: No unit records irrigated cropping; the evidence is applied here by default, and the cattle-shade units concern livestock rather than irrigated crops [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The only recorded country is Cuba (upper-middle income); the other five units have no country or income group, so the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies and rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The Ethiopian, German, Indian, Senegalese and Chinese units come from rainfed cropping, and the German unit is high-income temperate evidence; the yield gain applies to hot conditions only [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies and report cooling, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.mechanism: Tree shade physically cools the microclimate crops and livestock sit in: reviews report that over-storey shade moderates severe temperature effects (2–4°C) on understorey crops in wheat, coffee and silvopasture systems, that tree shading can lower ambient temperatures by 4°C and soil temperatures by 6–10°C, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields such as coffee and raise food-staple yield by lowering daytime temperature and heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. In mixed crop–livestock systems in Brazil, comparing eucalyptus agroforestry with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100%, with lower thermal-comfort index, black-globe humidity index and radiant thermal load throughout [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].
agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.conditionality: All but the Brazilian unit are reviews or an IPCC assessment chapter restating other studies' findings rather than measuring heat stress directly, so none of them name a country or farming system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The single primary measurement is upper-middle-income Brazilian silvopasture, outside the LIC/LMIC target, which is why the row transfers only as adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. No unit in this row measures a severe or extreme heat event.

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it (Ocampo et al. 2012) [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain (Abreu 2002) [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In Nicaragua, Betancourt et al. 2003 found milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun (Souza et al. 2000) [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. General reviews report the same cooling: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects in silvopasture as well as crop systems, and tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: Every unit reports a benefit, but none measures it in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, and the transfer to LIC/LMIC rangelands is not direct: almost all the weight sits in upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and unlocated reviews, with Nicaragua the only lower-middle-income site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures are associations with shade rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: The Colombian unit is a review citing an earlier study (Ocampo et al.) that reports animal comfort without a size, and the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself, though its comparison of woody-cover levels is cited from an earlier study [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Latin America, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.mechanism: Shade over tree crops lowers the temperature the crop experiences. Reviews report that over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, that tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C (Liu et al. 2019), that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress (Arenas-Corraliza et al. 2018; Sida et al. 2018), and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee (Rahn et al. 2014, 2018) [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A coffee review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress (Lin et al. 2008; Meylan et al. 2017), and the IPCC notes, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.conditionality: Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not say how much that cuts crop or income losses, so the class is slight: all units rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact, and none measures the effect in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme. The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees for coffee adds that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; they are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, while the general review statements are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies. The cocoa meta-analysis is weighted towards Ghana (lower-middle income), the Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high income, and several units have no country or income group, so the transfer to the LIC/LMIC target is adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Trees cool the air and soil that crops and livestock experience, through shade and altered radiation and humidity. In Ethiopia, air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under Faidherbia albida canopy compared with the open field, reaching a maximum of 29°C under the canopy against 36°C in the open, and temperature stayed above 28°C for about six hours a day in the open field against under two hours under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In Germany, poplar alley cropping measured 3.4°C lower air temperature than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found summer air temperature significantly reduced by 4.01% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees reduce the maximum daily temperature by an average of 1 to 2.5°C, with stronger effects on hotter, drier days, and under Acacia tortilis canopy in Senegal's Ferlo, air temperatures ranged from 29 to 36°C against 26 to 42°C outside the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. For livestock, the cooling under trees is reported to reduce heat stress directly: temperature under tree crowns in tropical pastures is 2 to 9°C lower than in open areas, with tree groups giving the largest reduction (3.6°C) and live fences the smallest (1.7°C) [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Brazil's Caatinga, the black-globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 to 84.2 and radiant thermal load also fell comparing shade under tree strips with sun exposure, and strips with the most woody cover were more efficient at mitigating cattle heat load than an almost treeless system, with the cooling effect holding even when the trees were leafless in the dry season [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]. In Brazilian silvopasture compared with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100% [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A Peru/Colombia systematic review reports silvopastoral systems reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13°C on the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. More recent evidence adds further confirmation across livestock and crop systems. A review of cattle shade attributes trees as the most effective shade for livestock, combining sunlight protection with evaporative cooling from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. Tree shading is reported to lower ambient temperatures by 4°C and soil temperatures by 6 to 10°C in tropical agroforestry, and shade trees are said to reduce canopy temperature by 2 to 4°C more generally, moderating severe temperature effects on understorey crops in wheat, coffee and silvopastoral systems [ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1]. In Costa Rica, measured shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7°C, with full-sun coffee leaves reaching up to 5°C above ambient air [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. CATIE reviews report tropical silvopasture 2 to 5°C cooler under tree crowns than outside them, and about 2°C cooler under tall (20 m) canopy specifically [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. For livestock specifically, reviews describe trees in paddocks shading animals and reducing heat stress, live fences in Cuba and the Neotropics re-purposed to shade cattle and improve comfort, reproduction, weight gain and milk production, and intensive shrub/tree/rotational-pasture systems in Colombia's dry Caribbean region reducing thermal stress and making animals calmer; a review of Brazilian silvopastoral studies found the effect on biophysical variables mostly (57%) positive, including lower air, black-globe and soil-surface temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. More general reviews describe shade trees buffering air and soil temperature, slowing wind speed and raising humidity and soil moisture under canopy, agroforestry and mulching protecting crops against extreme microclimate and soil-moisture swings, and shade trees stabilising coffee yield and raising food-staple yield by lowering daytime temperature and heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. In a high-shade Mexican coffee site, within-day temperature fluctuated the least and stayed closest to the 20°C optimum compared with medium- and low-shade sites [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured air temperature 1.3 °C and 1.2 °C cooler and soil-surface temperature 2.1 °C and 2.0 °C cooler than a 15-year-old monoculture, attributed to the alley crops' greater leaf area and ground cover intercepting radiation and reducing vertical mixing of warm air; against both the seven- and 15-year monocultures, the pepper and cacao alleys still measured significantly cooler soil-surface temperatures [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]. In Brazilian coffee, shaded plots measured consistently lower soil temperature at 10 cm depth than unshaded plots, and air temperature under shade had less day-to-day variation and a lower maximum than in the unshaded area [ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: Against this, one measured unit in Senegal finds windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots rather than cooling them, with variable impacts depending on crop and growth stage — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter adds that while shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee, the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In Ghana, cocoa shade trees were confirmed to moderate the microclimate especially during dry and extremely dry periods, but daily mean maximum air temperatures still reached up to 44°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. A Brazilian systematic review of silvopastoral thermal-comfort studies found most studies showed no significant difference in the temperature-humidity index between silvopastoral and treeless pasture, which the authors partly attribute to the index ignoring solar radiation — the main pathway through which trees reduce heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. In Mexican coffee, seasonal mean temperature (as opposed to day-to-day fluctuation) was not significantly different along a shade gradient [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. No unit in this row measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot-season or hot-day conditions [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The pooled evidence spans many countries across West Africa, East Africa, Latin America, South and East Asia, temperate Europe and Australia/the USA at every income level, so it transfers only as adjacent rather than squarely in context [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. One review also notes a different kind of downside: while shade improved microclimate stability in Central America, excessive shade combined with heavy rain raised fungal disease risk on the crop in parts of East Africa, a separate hazard from heat itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. None of this new evidence states a size with a country or farming-system attached in most cases — the livestock reviews are pantropical or regional rather than site-specific — so it does not change the row's existing adjacent transfer to the LIC/LMIC target. Against the cooling pattern, air temperature in the Malaysian pepper and cacao alleys did not differ from the age-matched seven-year-old monoculture, so the cooling shows up only against the older 15-year stand [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_2]; and bamboo and bactris alleys at the same site measured significantly hotter air (36.4 °C and 37.0 °C) than every other treatment, including both monocultures — a measured harm from the wrong alley crop, which the authors attribute to bamboo's sparse canopy, gaps and low ground cover leaving the soil exposed, concluding bamboo and bactris may not be appropriate intercrops for this reason [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. None of this newer evidence states a size with a country or farming-system that would move the row's existing adjacent-transfer reading: Malaysia and Brazil are both upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In Senegal's Ferlo, minimum and maximum air temperatures under the canopy of Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C, against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Both units are earlier studies cited in reviews and report air temperature under tree canopies, a component of heat-stress impact rather than a measured heat-stress outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In the Ferlo the canopy narrowed the range in both directions, with a higher minimum as well as a lower maximum under the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: In rainfed cropping, trees and shelterbelts cool the crop. Under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C against the open field, peaking at 29oC under the canopy versus 36oC outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland found shelterbelts reduced summer air temperature by 4.01% against unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1], and a review reports, second-hand, that poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: an FAO review in Senegal states, second-hand, that windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage, so shelter designs that cut wind may warm rather than cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The units measure air temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not heat-stress yield losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. They span low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal, upper-middle-income China and high-income Germany [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: In Brazil, eucalyptus–brachiaria agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture, and in semi-arid Kenya shade trees are cited as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations, which in turn can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Both units are cited statements from a review or a study's introduction rather than the sources' own measurements, and they report animal thermal comfort and microclimate, components of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. The Brazilian unit is upper-middle income and the Kenyan unit lower-middle income [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopastoral systems for dairy cows, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint and the dairy review rest on measurements [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the Cuban and Neotropical shade units repeat Fudora et al. and Harvey et al., the latter a reading of livestock keepers' knowledge rather than a measurement [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses, and the evidence is mainly from upper-middle-income Latin America with a high-income Costa Rican unit [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Trees associated with a crop buffer air and soil temperature, reduce wind speed, and increase air humidity and soil moisture under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. In a shade-by-drought experiment on cocoa in Ghana, sub-canopy temperatures were lower in shade than in full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: The tropical coffee and cacao synthesis gives a cited statement with no measurement or country [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. Both units report temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact, rather than crop losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__income.mechanism: Tree cover lowers air temperature in the units from high-income settings. A review reports, second-hand, that on hot summer days a poplar alley-cropping system in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than a sole wheat system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, a review reports, second-hand, that temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Costa Rican coffee, shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C against full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. A review of cattle heat stress drawing on Queensland and Californian work cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, combining protection from sunlight with cooling as moisture evaporates from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__income.conditionality: All units are from high-income settings (Germany, Costa Rica, Australia and the USA), outside the LIC/LMIC target, and they describe air temperature or shade cooling, components of heat-stress impact, rather than measured heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. The coffee unit is crop-specific to shaded coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4], and the cooling depends on tree arrangement, with live fences giving the smallest reduction [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The cattle-shade statement gives no tree system or density and is an old citation in a review, so it supports the direction only [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__income.mechanism: In Ethiopia, Faidherbia albida trees cut the radiation reaching the wheat canopy and made the wheat 6°C cooler than open wheat [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5]. In the Ferlo, Senegal, air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged less widely than outside the canopy, and in Kenya shade trees are described as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations and can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. In a shade-by-drought experiment on cocoa in Ghana, sub-canopy temperatures were lower in shade than in full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__income.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal pull the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots with impacts that depend on the crop and its growth stage, so the evidence pools opposite signs [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. All units are from LIC/LMIC countries (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Senegal); the review units are reported second-hand, and all rest on temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__biodivers.mechanism: Linear plantings add woody habitat structure to farmland. A tropical-agroforestry review states that, depending on their floristic diversity, structural complexity and management, windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species, including a limited number of forest-dependent species, by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. In Colombia and Costa Rica, farmers report that planting live fences increases landscape connectivity, creating local corridors that both fauna and flora can use, which they see as positive for native biodiversity conservation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. The same review also reports a mixed case: in Queensland, Australia, planted eucalyptus windbreaks were useful habitat for some bird species but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, and held much lower value as wildlife habitat than riparian vegetation, which the authors attribute to the windbreaks' lower structural complexity and single-species planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__biodivers.conditionality: The class stays slight because one of the three units finds no added value for mammals and forest specialists relative to riparian habitat, holding agreement at medium rather than high [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3]. None of the three states a size for the conservation gain: the windbreak review is a generalisation across cited temperate studies, the live-fence unit is a farmer-perception survey across Colombia and Costa Rica (upper-middle and high income), and neither names the countries, income group or farming system behind the pooled row, which is why confidence stays low and the row only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__carbon_se.mechanism: A systematic review of East African agroforestry reports that trees on boundaries hold 26.7 ± 14.1 Mg C ha−1 of above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__carbon_se.conditionality: This is a carbon stock, not an annual sequestration rate, and boundary planting is a linear practice, so a per-hectare density should not be multiplied over a pixel area [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5]. The evidence is from East Africa (LIC/LMIC) [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__drought__.mechanism: Live fences of fodder species such as Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and Erythrina poeppigiana supply high-quality livestock feed in the dry season, mainly when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__drought__.conditionality: This is a review reporting what other authors describe about dry-season livestock feed, not a measured drought-impact outcome, and the benefit is for livestock [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. It is a pantropical review with no country or income group recorded, so its fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__drought__.mechanism: Linear tree plantings have little direct drought evidence, and it points two ways. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply high-quality livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For crops, the FAO Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought: some studies find higher crop yields near windbreaks in drier years, while others judge the hedges could harm non-irrigated crops [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The engine reads this as a small benefit that is not quantified, discounted by the no-consensus finding.
agroforestry__linear_boundary__drought__.conditionality: The two units answer different questions. The gain is fodder for livestock from live fences [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; for field crops beside windbreaks the literature is split, as the Senegal review states [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. Which one matters depends on whether the farm's drought exposure is in its herd or its field crops. Both units are reviews with no effect sizes, and neither compares the same field with and without the trees in a severe or extreme drought. agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.mechanism: Linear tree plantings have been found both to raise and to lower yields. Gains come from shelter: windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% by protecting plants from winter desiccation, protected plots in the Senegal River valley showed a 23 per cent total yield increase in the off-season, crop yield was 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland in a Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis, and live fences can improve soil fertility and crop yields provided tree roots are deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows found they raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68), counted here as a component of the production gap; hedgerow litter and the capture of nutrient-laden sediment from runoff supply it [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Losses come from competition and shade: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], cereal yields next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years of a field study [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1], excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14], and in the West African Sahel live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Hedgerow intercropping in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis gave a response ratio of 0.9, an interval touching no effect [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. A global quantitative review of paddocks with windbreaks found yield reduced by 8.3% on average against paddocks with no windbreaks, excluding the land occupied by the trees, with more decreases (n = 171) than increases (n = 83): crop yield −9.2% and crop biomass −9.3%, while pasture showed a small average increase of +3.1% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. In the same Saskatchewan study the sheltered zone beyond the competition strip gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but against the mid-field yield the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, while doubting that baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The global review's distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature adds a further field/forage-crop verdict favouring shelter generally, with whole-field weighted mean yield gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]; within that literature, Canada/USA spring wheat yield was higher in the sheltered zone (1 to 15 tree heights) and the net field-level yield across the whole span was 3.5% above unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_kort88_4, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5]. In northeast China, shelterbelt-protected maize gained 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, the gain largest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. A Cambodian on-station trial of leucaena living fences adds further support: unirrigated leucaena still produced 2.8 to 6.5 kg of fresh fodder biomass per week per 100 trees right through the dry-season feed-gap period, and cattle supplemented with this fodder gained weight on average (4.2%) over a 107-day trial while control-group cattle fed only rice straw and local grass lost weight on average (0.7%) [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.conditionality: The evidence itself names most of what separates gains from losses. Distance from the trees: the same Chinese meta-analysis reports the field-scale gain and the edge-zone loss, which are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and in Senegal yields fell within 10 metres of the hedges in the rainy season while the protected plots as a whole gained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. Root depth: the live-fence benefit is conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Season: in the Saskatchewan study the sheltered-zone gain appeared in 1989 and 1990 but was absent in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, which the authors attribute to high actual evapotranspiration by the crops [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the Saskatchewan shelterbelt units are measured but high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. The hedgerow soil-nitrogen pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil concentration, not yield, so it shows a pathway to higher output rather than the output itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Against this, the same windbreak review notes that land occupied by the trees and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter gain into a net loss in some studies [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2], and its own Canada/USA wheat data show a 50% loss in the competition zone right next to the belt (0.5 to 1 tree heights), matching the Saskatchewan edge-zone loss already in this row [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3]. In northeast China, maize yield fell once shelterbelt density rose above the optimum, showing the same diminishing-returns pattern as the paddock-geometry and distance effects already described [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4]. None of the Chinese or Canada/USA figures names a country-level income group beyond upper-middle or high, so this additional evidence does not shift the row's existing LIC/LMIC transfer. The Cambodian living-fence trial has no significance test reported for either the fodder yield or the cattle weight-gain comparison, the leucaena was grown on-station rather than harvested from an actual fence line (the living-fence framing is the authors'), and there was no comparator arm for the fodder yield beyond the dry-season feed gap with no tree fodder at all [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.mechanism: Boundary and line plantings earn money from the tree products. A windbreak hedge in irrigated rice in the Senegal River valley had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent counting its woody products [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields of Haryana, India, a biodrainage review reports from Ram et al. (2011) that eucalyptus strip plantations on farm boundaries, which need only an initial investment, gave a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 over the first rotation through fodder, wood or fibre harvested [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. Neotropical farmers perceive live fences as a source of additional income, for example from timber sales [ev_household_income_moran18_7].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.conditionality: All the units are second-hand: the returns are financial indicators and the income claim a farmer perception, each used as a proxy for poverty, and none measures household poverty or how the gain is shared [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3, ev_household_income_moran18_7]. The strength is therefore not quantified. Both financial results come from irrigated systems (rice in Senegal, wheat inter-spaces in canal-irrigated Haryana), in lower-middle-income countries within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]; in the Haryana case the trees were planted to drain waterlogged land, so the return comes with that purpose [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.mechanism: Live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used in Colombia, Mexico and Nigeria to prevent erosion and retain soil moisture, live fences in India reduce erosion by lowering runoff velocity, and Kenyan farmers report that planting trees in a line prevents soil being swept away by water [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. A global review of plot and field studies found linear tree plantings (windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows) cut soil loss by 55% on average against land without them, the lowest of the agroforestry systems compared though the differences among systems were not significant [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, windbreak patches reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.conditionality: Only the compiled review and the Chinese windbreak measurement state a size; the live-fence and lined-tree citations and the Kenyan farmer's account give no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The 55% figure is an average of compiled study reductions across temperate and tropical sites, not a weighted meta-analytic effect, and it is not specific to low-income settings [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers rather than stating a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The Chinese windbreak measurement is upper-middle-income evidence, adding to the mix already in this row [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The pooled countries span high-income Canada, upper-middle-income China, and lower-middle-income India and Kenya, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target rather than squarely in context.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.mechanism: Windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows on farmland hold soil and nutrients on the field through surface cover and fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies found linear tree plantings decreased the average nutrient loss from leaching and runoff by 16% and 33% respectively, against land without them [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.conditionality: Confidence is very low: the row rests on a single review with few case studies for linear plantings, the percentages are averages of compiled study results rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, and no country or income group is given [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The ranges across studies are wide and include no change: phosphorus losses fell by 0–50%, and the nitrogen range runs from an increase to a large decrease [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The review also reports that linear plantings reduced nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium losses less than the other agroforestry systems it covered. The unit measures nutrient loss leaving the field, which is the pathway to water quality downstream, not stream or groundwater quality itself.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.mechanism: One study links field shelterbelts to more water stress, through less soil water next to the trees. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The engine reads a slight, unquantified increase in water stress; the counterfactual is soil further into the same field, not an unsheltered field.
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.conditionality: This rests on one source. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Missing: measured soil water or crop water stress beside windbreaks, live fences or hedgerows in low- or lower-middle-income settings, and any study that compares sheltered with unsheltered fields.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.mechanism: Deep-rooted, fast-growing boundary trees can drain waterlogged fields by transpiring excess soil water (biodrainage). A review of biodrainage cites a study by Ram et al. (2011) in canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, Haryana, India: parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis along farm boundaries, spaced at 66 m at a density of 300 plants per hectare, lowered the groundwater table beneath the strips by 85 cm compared with adjacent unvegetated fields in 3 years, with wheat grown between the strips [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.conditionality: No class is set because the row rests on one second-hand reading of one Indian study. What is missing is a second independent source or a direct measurement, ideally one that reports crop yield or farm income on the drained land rather than water-table depth alone; the water-table fall is measured under the strips, and how far it extends into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind speed over a zone that typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large landscapes need multiple barriers to control wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. Live fences in India serve as windbreaks and raise soil moisture retention through litter build-up [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: Both units are reviews citing earlier studies and concern wind erosion and sheltering, not cyclone damage [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. Only the Indian unit names a country (lower-middle income) [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: None of the five units measures a severe or extreme wind or cyclone event — the evidence covers routine wind and erosion control. Only the Chinese shelterbelt study states a size; the rest describe mechanism or role without a magnitude, which caps the class at moderate. The Chinese unit is upper-middle income, the Senegalese and Indian units lower-middle income, so the row sits adjacent to, not squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.conditionality: The strong class rests on a single trial and a single taxon: earthworm diversity is a soil-biodiversity indicator, not a measure of wider farm or landscape biodiversity, and statistical significance of the difference is not reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. The system was fertilised and given need-based irrigation at tree establishment, so the result applies to managed alley systems on degraded lateritic soils in lower-middle-income settings; further studies, on other taxa, are needed before this reads as a general effect.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.mechanism: Trees planted into cropland add carbon to the soil through leaf litter, prunings and roots, raising soil carbon storage above that of the crop grown alone. In a ten-year trial on degraded red and lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon under a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system reached 0.59% against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from an initial 0.30% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, consistent with earlier syntheses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. In southern Malawi, Tephrosia vogelii relay-planted under maize keeps growing into the dry season and returns nitrogen-rich leafy residues; at Songani soil C under this intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.conditionality: The direction is consistent, but not every site shows a clear gain. The Malawi difference was a trend that was not significant (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1], and at Sadore, Niger, the block with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held from 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without after four years of millet and cowpea, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. The Niger trial compares two blocks with tree presence neither randomised nor replicated, so block differences are mixed into the contrast [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Soil carbon is a component of carbon removal, measured here as a stock or concentration, not as a removal rate, and tree biomass storage is not counted in this row [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. The strongest gain comes from a long-running research-station trial on degraded soil, where the starting carbon was low [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. The field evidence is from low-income Malawi and Niger and lower-middle-income India, all rainfed cropping; the meta-analysis is global [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Rwanda, where the arm was tree-planting agroforestry, cost $201 per household [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one low-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. The same quote attributes Rwanda's higher per-household cost than Ghana's FMNR to tree-planting agroforestry where average land size per household is much more limited [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

The same quote notes the much more limited average land size per household in Rwanda and gives $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana [ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: Planted tree-crop systems in annual cropping add labour, and costs rise with it. In Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping in a maize/groundnut intercrop raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%), and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In Nigeria, maize plots mulched with tree prunings required higher labour input than the fertilizer and untreated controls, 96% of it for collecting and managing mulch and only 4% for weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model adds two further labour-cost readings, both increases: annual labour for maize production under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is reported increased by 53 percent against the traditional bush-fallow control, because of the added labour for hedgerow pruning, and under the closer 2 m spacing the model assumes total labour increases by 87 percent, since more hedgerows need pruning [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: The cost rise comes from the work of cutting, carrying and spreading prunings, so the design and harvest regime of the hedgerows set the bill [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and they decreased from the first to the third year, so the 34% is an average that is heavier early on [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In the Nigerian trial the trees were grown on a separate plot and the prunings carried in, a biomass-transfer design rather than trees in the field itself [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both are on-station or researcher-run trials in lower-middle-income West and Central Africa; the size rests on the Cameroon figure alone, and neither unit is a cost saving. Both readings add to the cost-increase side of this row rather than the cost-saving side: like the Cameroon and Nigeria mulching evidence already here, the extra labour is pruning and handling tree biomass, not time saved on weeding. The 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier cited labour study rather than measured by the modelling authors themselves, and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption (more hedgerows to prune at closer spacing), not a measurement. Both are lower-middle-income Nigerian evidence, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: Within planted silvoarable systems, trees are reported to help crops reach water and recover from drought stress. In the Sahel, hydraulic redistribution is reported to let crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and millet intercropped with the woody shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping system, crop losses occurred only in the monocrop, not in the agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, said deep-rooted mango, papaya and banana trees get water from deep down and do not dry up fast, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1].
