agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__produ.mechanism: Fertiliser-tree and planted-alley systems raise crop yield and revenue across many Sahelian and sub-Saharan African sites. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yield by 41% in the unfertilised control and by 10% with farmyard manure, and raised gross crop revenue 5 to 14% excluding fruit, 2 to 3-fold once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree (Gliricidia-based) adopters had a 35% higher value of food-crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their modelled counterfactual [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1]. In Kenya, improved fallow (planted fertiliser trees) raised mean maize yield 128% (median 167%) over a no-input control [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A meta-analysis across West, East and southern Africa put the maize-yield response ratio at 1.27-1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11-1.3 with relay intercrops against unfertilised maize, with a 1.6 t/ha gain from coppicing species [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis separately found crop-yield response ratios of 2.1 for alley cropping, 1.3 for dispersed tree intercropping and 2.6 for planted/improved fallow against non-agroforestry controls [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_4, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_6]. In Cameroon, alley-cropped maize and groundnut out-yielded treeless controls across the trial years without added fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. In maize-Gliricidia trials in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave more stable yields than monoculture maize across long-term seasons, and an intercrop with half the recommended fertiliser matched fully fertilised monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. In India, wheat grain yield rose 6.8% from reduced heat load under Populus deltoides [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In Ethiopia, land productivity improved rapidly on about a fifth to a third of sites visited where nitrogen-fixing Acacia decurrens was incorporated into the farming system [ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_2]. A Nigerian economic model of alley cropping on a 7% slope near Ibadan projects that, because lower cumulative soil loss sustains yield over a 20-year horizon, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping maintains the highest relative maize yield of five compared land-management systems, ahead of 4 m alley cropping, no-till and two bush-fallow rotations [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__produ.conditionality: The benefit is conditional on fertiliser treatment in the same Niger trial: the Ziziphus gain reversed to a 13% millet loss and a 4 to 11% loss for the millet/cowpea intercrop once NPK fertiliser was applied, and cowpea alone lost 15% without fertiliser (probably from tree shade), though it gained 9% with NPK (nitrogen from Ziziphus residues); soil total nitrogen did not differ significantly with and without the trees [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. At Msekera, Zambia, fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize-Gliricidia intercrop, and two of three stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. In Malawi, a Tephrosia relay intercrop (leafy residues, no grain) gave the same maize grain yield as monoculture maize fertilised the same way, so no yield gain from the relay crop itself [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. In Kenya, the long-rains production-function estimate for improved fallow was not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6]. Young, widely-spaced trees compete hard with the crop: in China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield 46.03% and alfalfa hay 51.83% against sole cropping, partly from less cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; a review of alley systems found a mean paddock-level yield reduction of 17.63% (SD 36%, though 69 of 333 responses were increases), a predicted loss of more than 25% at spacings under 2.5 tree heights between alleys, and a 13% gain only at the widest spacing (15 tree heights) tested [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]; and in Kenya, tree-crop water competition under Grevillea robusta delayed maize flowering and development and could cause crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. In France, a walnut-alley trial recorded winter pea yield consistently lower than the full-sun control, by 25 to 77% under normal rainfall and 1 to 47% under an imposed spring drought [ev_crop_yield_blan22_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_2]. In China and Indonesia, intercropping cut wheat and third-harvest maize yield respectively against monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazil, agroforestry soybean yielded only 500-700 kg/ha against about 2700-3000 kg/ha in monoculture [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Mozambique, a PES tree-planting intervention showed a negative crop-value proxy, against a strongly positive one for Malawi's fertiliser-tree programme in the same review [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3]. A cross-regional review found trees had a negative effect on crop yields in 33% of African, 48% of Asian and 33% of American studies, even though the majority (52%) of cases overall were net positive or neutral, and it is based mostly (53 of 58 agroforestry studies) on trees introduced to open fields rather than agroforestry retained under a forest canopy [ev_crop_yield_reed17_1, ev_crop_yield_reed17_2, ev_crop_yield_reed17_3]. Most of the gain evidence (Niger, Malawi, Kenya, Cameroon, Ethiopia, the sub-Saharan meta-analyses) sits inside the LIC/LMIC target; the French, Chinese and some Indonesian/Iranian units are upper-middle or high income, outside it [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_place05_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. The Nigerian alley-cropping yield ranking is modelled rather than measured, running a simplified erosion model through a yield-loss function, and the alley yields are expressed per unit of cropped land only, not discounted for the land the hedgerows themselves occupy [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for 4 years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. In Ethiopia, market-oriented agroforestry with Acacia decurrens is credited with income, employment and reduced poverty in supported microwatersheds [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. On-station and on-farm trials that cost both systems show trees with crops earning more than either alone: in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave a net benefit of US$4148 per hectare against US$2386 for the traditional treeless maize/groundnut intercrop [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]; in North Kordofan, Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal gum plantation out-earned the same crops grown alone: sorghum gave a net revenue of 558 SDG per hectare against 501 SDG as a sole crop, sesame 300 against 205, and roselle 518 against 389 [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]; and in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system gave net returns 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a 10-year cycle, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. In southwestern Nigeria, a sweet orange orchard intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus had a net present value of N 154300 and one intercropped with cassava and maize N 105900, against N -37900 for the monocropped orchard, which yielded no revenue in its first years while the intercropped plots earned throughout [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. Trees can also compensate for crop losses: a review of 74 articles found the share of studies reporting harm fell from 36% for yield to 16% for overall livelihood effects, and where trees raised food yield the livelihood effect was positive in 86% of studies [ev_household_income_reed17_1, ev_household_income_reed17_2, ev_household_income_reed17_3]. In Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot intercrops gave a higher average cash flow than sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. A Nigerian economic model of alley cropping near Ibadan compares the present value of incremental net returns (PVINR) of Leucaena alley cropping against a traditional bush-fallow control over a multi-decade horizon. At the model's base-case discount rate, both 2 m and 4 m alley spacings show a positive incremental return against the control across the population-density scenarios tested, though in each scenario a long bush-fallow rotation still comes out ahead of alley cropping where land is abundant [ev_economic_return_ehui90_7, ev_economic_return_ehui90_8, ev_economic_return_ehui90_9, ev_economic_return_ehui90_10].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.conditionality: The gains depend on land, labour and input costs, and some adopters lose. In south-western Nigeria, mulching maize with leaves cut and carried from a multipurpose-tree plot gave higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer only when the land under the trees was not valued; where land is scarce the technology is unprofitable in both the short and long term [ev_economic_return_korm99_5, ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In West Bengal the benefit–cost ratio of sole pigeon pea was higher than that of pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, so the higher net return came with higher costs [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. Several effects did not reach significance or reversed: Zambian improved fallows raised maize income but not total crop income, Kenyan improved fallows changed liquid assets but not significantly, and crop–fruit tree intercropping in China (Dai et al., 2017) lowered gross income [ev_household_income_castle21s_4, ev_household_income_castle21s_5, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; in western Kenya small farm sizes limited the impact of improved fallows on poverty even though they were attractive to the poor [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are net returns or net present values from research-managed trials, components of household income rather than measured poverty change [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Nigerian orchard compares trees with crops against trees alone, so it shows the value of the crops in the alleys rather than of adding trees to a field [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Ethiopian unit is an evaluation lesson rather than a measured effect [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. The Zambian figures are an earlier study cited in an ICRAF working paper and compare losses on crop failure rather than incomes [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. At a higher, sensitivity discount rate representing credit-constrained subsistence farmers, the same 2 m alley-cropping system reverses to a negative incremental return, less profitable than the more erosive bush-fallow control; the authors attribute this to alley cropping's establishment cost, since the Leucaena hedgerows take up to two years before giving any benefit — a measured harm the engine counts for some adopters alongside the other losses already in this row [ev_economic_return_ehui90_11]. These present-value rankings are ordinal figures in Nigerian naira against the bush-fallow control, not comparable in absolute terms to the other currency figures already in this row, and all are modelled rather than measured, running a simplified erosion model through the same SCUAF framework used elsewhere in this register.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.mechanism: Trees combined with crops, as alley cropping or contour hedgerow intercropping, protect the soil surface with living plants, litter and mulch and bind it with extended fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies against sole crops found silvoarable agroforestry cut soil loss by 66% on average and water loss by 43% [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.conditionality: The review-based average rests on a single review whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and which gives no country or income-group breakdown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. The newer field and modelled evidence now carries most of the weight in this row and points the same way: in Nigeria, a modelled 2 m alley-cropping system gives the lowest predicted 20-year cumulative soil loss of the systems compared, and in the Philippines, a hillside field trial found soil loss fall from 124 to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added to the farmer's practice, falling further to 3 and then 0.2 t/ha/yr as mulch and zero tillage were added on top [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3]. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. In China, mean soil loss per rainfall event fell with both younger and older intercropped trees against mono-cropped peanut, but mean runoff per event was higher in both tree treatments than in the mono-crop — a reversal the authors attribute to surface seals forming on the untilled soil near the trees rather than to the trees raising runoff generally [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: In rainfed cropland, the measured evidence points both ways depending on whether water-use efficiency or soil moisture itself is measured. At Sadore in the Nigerien Sahel, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in millet fields raised the rainwater-use efficiency of millet by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In a long-running Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, system water-use efficiency (above-ground biomass including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) was strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At the same site, available soil water was also greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase in two seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation, and higher below 60 cm in the second season's May reading [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: Against this, at the start of the cropping season available soil water was generally lower in the tree-based Makoka systems, consistent with the trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5]; several other season-level readings found no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with the associated crop. In France, a walnut-alley trial found a depth split: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. The water-use-efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of water use, not grain per unit of water, so the tree's own biomass lifts the tree-system values; the Niger figures, by contrast, count crop biomass only per mm of rainfall, so they show the crop itself using rain more efficiently with trees nearby [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]. The German and French units are high-income temperate evidence, each from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Niger and Malawi evidence (low income) sits inside it, which is why this row transfers in_context overall. This Chinese result is the deciding addition for this row: benefit and harm/no-effect units in this sub-practice were already close in weight, split between the water-use-efficiency gains (which credit the tree's own biomass, not just the crop's) and the direct soil-moisture readings that show trees depleting water at the start of the season. Adding this one further harm reading — drier soil profiles under intercropped trees than under mono-cropped peanut — is now enough to tip the balance from a row that read a moderate net benefit into one where neither side has enough weight to set a direction, which is why the class changes to conflicting evidence rather than staying a moderate gain. This is upper-middle-income Chinese evidence, consistent with the row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth, as a review reports from Dhillon et al. (2010) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: the only evidence is a single Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review, with no size stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look. The study system is irrigated cropping, applied here to all farming systems by default [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].

What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__production_gap.mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. In lowland Kenya, steers given incremental supplements of gliricidia (Gliricidia sepium) and leucaena forage alongside Napier grass gained 57% more live weight than steers fed Napier grass alone once the tree-legume forage reached 27% of total dry-matter intake [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_3]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. More recent additions to this evidence pool mostly repeat the same pattern. In Kenya, improved-fallow soil-fertility trials raised maize yield by a mean of 128% against no-input plots (median 167%), close to the 114% mean for biomass transfer and above the 89% mean for mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found soil available nitrogen 46% higher under agroforestry than crop monocultures, with a mean response ratio of 1.46 [ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_2]. In Brazil, cassava under tree cover yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha against zero for the unshaded monoculture control in one season [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a review of coconut-based systems in Sri Lanka reports increased nut yields when pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee are intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1]. More recent evidence adds further detail on shelterbelt and windbreak systems. In northeast China, shelterbelt-protected maize gained 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, largest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature finds field and forage crop yield generally higher in sheltered fields, with whole-field weighted mean gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it, and a net field-level spring wheat gain of 3.5% in Canada/USA once the competition zone, occupied land and sheltered zone are combined [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis gives crop-yield response ratios by agroforestry type: 2.1 for alley cropping, 1.3 for dispersed tree intercropping and 2.6 for planted/improved fallow against non-agroforestry controls, with soil total nitrogen also raised (response ratio 1.2), and the proportion of observations showing a yield gain ranging from 5% for hedgerow intercropping up to 93% for biomass transfer [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_4, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_kuyah19_1, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_7]. A review of 21 studies found 15 with higher yield in agroforestry, 5 higher in monoculture and 1 showing no significant difference, framing the land-equivalent-ratio case that monoculture would need 25-74% more land for the same output, with agroforestry 36-100% more productive by that measure; in Iran, wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher in intercropped systems near trees than in the respective monocultures, and in Bolivia total cocoa-system production was three times higher in agroforestry than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]. In the Sahel, a review across nine countries found millet and sorghum yields often higher near shrubs (range -25 to +120%), though more variable near trees (range -100 to +200%, i.e. complete crop failure to tripling), and soil nitrogen 38% higher under scattered shrubs than in open fields in semi-arid Niger [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_felix18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1]. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that in treeless areas, tree leaves, fruit and pods supply about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition, access to cool zones under trees is reported to raise livestock productivity by reducing heat stress, and soil total nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium under Faidherbia albida canopy rose 50%, 21% and 32% respectively over treeless areas [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. Across the Sahel, pooled FMNR adoption data show higher total crop production per hectare for low-intensity versus new or young FMNR, though the gain was not found for continuous, longer-established practice [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5, ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. In Brazil, silvopasture cattle gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. A Nigerian economic model of alley cropping on a 7% slope near Ibadan projects that, because lower cumulative soil loss sustains yield over a 20-year horizon, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping maintains the highest relative maize yield of five compared land-management systems, ahead of 4 m alley cropping, no-till and two bush-fallow rotations [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4]. A Cambodian on-station trial of leucaena living fences adds further support: unirrigated leucaena still produced 2.8 to 6.5 kg of fresh fodder biomass per week per 100 trees right through the dry-season feed-gap period, and cattle supplemented with this fodder (about 29% of their diet) gained weight on average (4.2%) over a 107-day trial while control-group cattle fed only rice straw and local grass lost weight on average (0.7%) [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1]. In Ghana, cocoa yield was 13% higher under moderate-shade hybrid cocoa than under full-sun hybrid cocoa [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2].
agroforestry__production_gap.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems now lean to a gain, but still record tree–crop competition losses next to the fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt study is measured, but it is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; its net loss is measured against the mid-field yield rather than an unsheltered field, a baseline the authors themselves question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. At Sadore the Ziziphus gain depended on the fertiliser: millet yield fell by 13 % under the trees with NPK, intercropped millet fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK and manure, and cowpea fell by 15 % in the unfertilised control, probably from tree shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; soil N there did not differ significantly with and without the trees, and tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated across the two blocks [ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Young fruit trees compete hard: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated semi-arid Xinjiang, China (upper-middle income), soybean yield fell by 46.03% and alfalfa by 51.83% against sole crops, partly because the intercrop had a smaller cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Sileshi maize meta-analysis compares against unfertilised maize, not farmer practice with fertiliser, and its authors note signs of publication bias [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1]; the hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Among the units added since the last round, several further losses and reversals appear. A global quantitative review found no significant difference in yield across three yield types (crop, crop biomass, pasture) sheltered by trees, with crop yield down 9.2% and crop biomass down 9.3% on average, and only pasture yield showing a small average increase (+3.1%) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3]. In Costa Rica, coffee under Erythrina shade of 40-60% cover produced 41% fewer fruits per tree than coffee under a maximum of 20% shade cover (1091 against 1838 fruits) [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1], and a further Costa Rican shade-coffee comparison found a 30% yield reduction under agroforestry against monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In Bolivia, cocoa productivity was on average 41% higher in monoculture than in agroforestry, though the authors note agroforestry revenues economically compensate for the difference [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1.5 t/ha are not compatible with carbon storage (shade) above 100-150 t C/ha, and storage above that level caps accessible yield at about 750 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6]. A standardised-mean-difference review finds effect sizes ranging from −0.33 for a payments-for-ecosystem-services programme in Nicaragua to 3.85 for improved fallows raising crop value in Malawi — an enormous spread within one review — and, in a certification-scheme comparison, Organic and Utz coffee certification were associated with statistically significant yield reductions (Hedges' g −0.488 and −0.465) while three other certification schemes showed insignificant increases [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. In Senegal, groundnut response under parkland tree canopy is reported variable with no consistent direction across studies, and windbreak hedges are reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield at Bambey [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. Several of this newer evidence base's gains are paired with losses in the same source. The same Chinese shelterbelt study and the northeast China maize study both show yield falling once protection rises above the optimal level or into the competition zone right next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4], and the windbreak-literature review notes that land occupation and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter gain into a net loss in some studies, with Canada/USA spring wheat yield 50% lower in the competition zone (0.5 to 1 tree heights from the belt) even though the net field-level yield across the whole sheltered span still came out 3.5% ahead [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2, ev_crop_yield_kort88_3]. In China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield 46.03% and alfalfa hay 51.83% against sole cropping over two years, partly because the intercrop had less cropped area and a lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In Indonesia, maize yield in an agroforestry system was significantly lower by the third harvest though soybean yield there was unaffected across all three harvests [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. A cross-regional review found trees had a negative effect on crop yields in 33% of African, 48% of Asian and 33% of American studies even though the majority (52%) of cases overall were net positive or neutral, and the review is based mostly (53 of 58 agroforestry studies) on trees introduced to open fields rather than retained under a forest canopy [ev_crop_yield_reed17_1, ev_crop_yield_reed17_2, ev_crop_yield_reed17_3]. In Brazil, drought-induced cocoa yield loss showed no relationship with shade-tree ground cover (p = 0.64), and in Mexico coffee harvest loss was unrelated to vegetation management, with all farms losing 18 to 40% of the harvest regardless of shade complexity [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Kenya, the long-rains production-function estimate for improved fallow was not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6], and in Ethiopia land productivity improved in only about a fifth to a third of sites visited where nitrogen-fixing Acacia decurrens was planted, not the majority [ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_2]. In Kerala/India, coconut yield showed no strong adverse impact from interplanted trees except where the trees directly shade the palms, and galangal rhizome yield showed no difference with or without over-canopy [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3]. A coffee meta-regression found shade density, region, species and year did not significantly explain the variance in effect size across pooled studies, so the pooled averages in this row mask considerable site-to-site variation [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9], and a separate coffee meta-analysis found yields declined above 60% shade, with 30-60% judged optimal — a dose-response ceiling rather than a one-way benefit [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3]. Live-fence yield gains are conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11], and soil-nitrogen gains from agroforestry show no significant difference by soil texture in one meta-analysis moderator test [ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_4]. Trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services exist in most agroforestry systems, though a review argues many systems are still far enough below their yield potential that this need not bind in practice [ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The Nigerian alley-cropping yield ranking is modelled, not measured: it runs a simplified erosion model through a separate yield-loss function rather than observing yields directly, and the alley yields are expressed per unit of cropped land only, not discounted for the land the hedgerows themselves occupy [ev_crop_yield_ehui90_4]. The Cambodian living-fence trial has no significance test reported for either the fodder yield or the cattle weight-gain comparison, the leucaena was grown on-station rather than harvested from an actual fence line (the living-fence framing is the authors'), and there was no comparator arm for the fodder yield beyond the dry-season feed gap with no tree fodder at all [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1]. Against this, in a newly-established US silvopasture, total forage dry matter was significantly lower under silvopasture than open pasture in the first year (255 against 409 kg/ha), attributed to volunteer grasses being slower to colonise the silvopasture, a competition effect the authors tie to shading and fewer open microsites; by the second year the difference was no longer significant, with the authors cautioning their small trial lacked power to detect a real difference [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1, ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_2]. In a longer-running New Zealand silvopasture, understorey pasture showed positive complementarity with the young pines at first, but this diminished as the trees matured and came to dominate soil moisture, and by about 15 years into the pine rotation the pasture had disappeared entirely from under the trees — a measured loss of the pasture itself, not just a yield reduction [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. The Ghanaian cocoa gain is modelled and confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the shade clusters it compares; the US and New Zealand forage results are measured but come from single, high-income temperate silvopasture trials, adding further support to the row's existing conflicting-evidence reading rather than resolving it [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2, ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1, ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Parkland trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, crucial in the dry season and during drought, and in Senegal access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected by tree cover [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Cereals lose out: grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, so the net effect depends on which crops dominate [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies from the Sahel and Senegal, and the fodder and livestock gains are stated without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light. Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The class rests on a single Chinese experiment with young trees, so confidence is low and the size may not hold as the trees mature or in other designs [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Part of the Chinese loss reflects the smaller cropped area and the lower seeding rate and irrigation given to the intercropped soybean, and yields are per unit of total plot area, so the tree rows count against the crop [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. The Senegal result runs the other way over the whole protected plot, which separates the two: hedges bordering a plot lose crop near the hedge but can raise the plot total, while trees planted through the plot at close spacing take crop area and water directly [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading in grey literature with no comparator stated beyond the unprotected plots. China is upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target; Senegal is lower-middle income, within it [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock systems, agroforestry's production gains come from several pathways. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had an average value of food crop production 35% higher than their counterfactual and maize productivity 32% higher [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1]. In Kenya's Lower Nyando, agroforestry-project farmers raised farm productivity by about 1,500 Ksh (US$19) a year more than a matched control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Across the Sahel (Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Senegal), moving from low-intensity to young-level farmer-managed natural regeneration significantly raised crop production and food consumption [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5]. In Brazilian silvopasture, cattle gained an average of 512 g of bodyweight per animal per day against 452 g/day in monoculture, a 60 g/day difference, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear/buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser cost [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. A Cambodian on-station trial of leucaena living fences adds further support: unirrigated leucaena still produced 2.8 to 6.5 kg of fresh fodder biomass per week per 100 trees right through the dry-season feed-gap period, and cattle supplemented with this fodder gained weight on average (4.2%) over a 107-day trial while control-group cattle fed only rice straw and local grass lost weight on average (0.7%) [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The class is capped at moderate rather than strong because only two of the nine units pointing this way state a size for the gain (the Malawi and Brazilian figures); the Kenyan, Sahelian and soil-nitrogen units describe direction without a comparable magnitude or, for Kenya, with standard errors the authors call large (P = 0.678) [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_bina15_5, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Set against this, the same Malawi study finds non-adopters would be worse off if they adopted fertilizer trees — a decrease in productivity, significant for the value of food production though not for maize — which the engine counts as measured harm for some adopters [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2]. A second Sahelian comparison, moving from low to continuous FMNR, found no significant difference, which the authors attribute to tree density and species quality rather than regeneration itself [ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. The Malawi figures come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, a conflict-of-interest the engine does not discount for the direction of this class but is noted here [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1]. The Cambodian living-fence trial has no significance test reported for either the fodder yield or the cattle weight-gain comparison, the leucaena was grown on-station rather than harvested from an actual fence line (the living-fence framing is the authors'), and there was no comparator arm for the fodder yield beyond the dry-season feed gap with no tree fodder at all [ev_forage_productivity_gill20_1, ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover consistently raises forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that measured in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain generally [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4], and in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture compared with low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, raised milk per hectare per year under Leucaena against an open-field system, and a review reports beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing, also higher than improved treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture is also reported to raise stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing, with proportional gains in meat and milk output, and better cattle feeding in critical drought periods is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant, giving more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Gains are not universal. Under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field, showing tree density itself can flip the sign [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral thermal-comfort and production studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia still lost milk production, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site forage evidence is the clearest statement that the benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. Most of the Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the clearest primary magnitudes (Colombia, Nicaragua, Costa Rica) are upper-middle or high income, while the Senegalese fodder evidence is lower-middle income, which is why this row's evidence sits adjacent to, rather than squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa change crop yield in both directions. They protect the crop from heat, add mulch and nitrogen and can steady yields between years, and several studies find equal or higher yields under moderate shade [ev_crop_yield_asare18_1, ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2, ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1]. They also compete with the crop for light and water: cocoa yields were lower in agroforestry than in monocultures, shaded coffee produced less fruit under dense Erythrina shade, and yields declined above about sixty percent shade [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. Where water is scarce, tree–crop competition for soil water intensifies [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Shade level separates the two sides: moderate shade tends to hold or raise yields, while dense shade lowers the main crop's yield. Total system output (crop plus timber, fruit and other products) is often higher even where the main crop yields less [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9], so a production-gap reading should state whether it counts the main crop only or the whole system. In dry or water-limited sites, plan for competition.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In high-income settings, agroforestry has been found both to raise and to lower output. Gains: in subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]; cited studies from Cañas, Costa Rica found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than in full sun and dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]; and a cited Costa Rican study found moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to, or 3% higher than, full sun [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]. Losses: a cited Costa Rican experiment recorded a 30% coffee yield reduction in the shaded system against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. A review of the worldwide windbreak literature adds a further measured contrast in Canada/USA spring wheat: yield in the competition zone right next to the belt (0.5 to 1 tree heights) fell 50% relative to unsheltered yield, yield in the sheltered zone further out (1 to 15 tree heights) was higher than unsheltered, and the net field-level yield across the whole 15-tree-height span, combining occupied land, the competition zone and the sheltered zone, was still 3.5% higher than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_4, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: What separates the sides is the system and the competition for resources. The gains are livestock under tree cover and windbreak-sheltered vegetables in Ontario, where the plots were irrigated from ditches, whereas the losses are crops competing with trees: cereal next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts and established shade over coffee [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. Distance from the trees and the season separate them within the shelterbelt study: yields were depressed next to the belt every year, higher in the sheltered zone in 1989 and 1990, and showed no sheltered gain in the wet 1991 season [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Costa Rican coffee several units find no difference: a case study recorded no negative yield effect of shade, systems under 30 % shade cover did not differ in yield from full sun with management intensity driving yield instead, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]. All units are from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; most are earlier findings read second-hand through reviews, while the Ontario result was measured directly but at a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt units were measured in the field; their net loss uses the mid-field yield as the reference, a baseline the authors question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The coffee units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In France, a walnut-alley trial recorded a consistent loss rather than a split by distance: winter pea yield was 25 to 77% lower than the full-sun control under normal rainfall and 1 to 47% lower under imposed spring drought, in both cases across the shade gradient from the tree line outward [ev_crop_yield_blan22_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_2]. The Canada/USA windbreak review is consistent with the Saskatchewan shelterbelt study already in this row: a loss right next to the trees, a gain further out, and, once the whole sheltered span is counted, a small net gain. The French result and the windbreak review are both high-income evidence (France, Canada, USA), consistent with the rest of this row, which sits outside the LIC/LMIC target throughout. A newly-established silvopasture trial in New York adds a further measured loss to this high-income scope row: total forage dry matter was significantly lower under silvopasture than open pasture in the first year after establishment (255 against 409 kg/ha), attributed to volunteer grasses struggling to colonise under the retained trees, though the difference was no longer significant by the second year [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1, ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_2]. In a longer-running New Zealand silvopasture, understorey pasture showed early complementarity with the young pines but disappeared entirely from under the trees by about 15 years into the rotation, as the maturing trees came to dominate soil moisture [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. Both are single-site, high-income temperate silvopasture trials, consistent with the pattern of competition losses this scope row already records. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica — the same high-income country as several of the other Costa Rican findings already in this scope row reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: A review of the worldwide windbreak literature finds field and forage crop yield generally higher in sheltered fields than unsheltered ones, with whole-field weighted mean yield gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% in regions without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]. A hedgerow meta-analysis found soil total nitrogen significantly higher under plant hedgerows than in farmland without them, attributed to hedgerow litter inputs and capture of nutrient-laden runoff [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: Set against this, the same windbreak review notes that land occupied by the trees and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter yield gain into a net loss in some studies [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2], and a coffee/cocoa review found dry-bean yield per hectare 26% lower under shade than in conventional, unshaded systems [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. None of the climate-zone windbreak figures gives a country, and they are weighted averages across many studies rather than a single measured site, so the practical gain for a given field is not guaranteed [ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]. The hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil nitrogen, a component of the production gap, not yield itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. All units in this scope row report a 'mixed' income classification (pooling evidence across several income bands in the source itself) rather than a single country or income group, so the row cannot be placed more precisely within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In upper-middle-income contexts, several studies show agroforestry or silvopasture raising production. In China, a national meta-analysis found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1], and a separate study of shelterbelt-protected maize in northeast China found yield gains of 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, highest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. In Iran, intercropped wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher near trees than in their respective monocultures [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing in the same year [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. For livestock, Colombian intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also allowed irrigation to be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Leucaena-based silvopasture in Colombia raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and a review reports silvopasture beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser costs [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7].
