Against the carbon gains above, a global synthesis found net soil CH4 emissions increased with a shift from agriculture to shaded perennial-crop systems — the opposite of the reduction seen for other agroforestry types — attributed to nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing shade trees inhibiting CH4 oxidation, though the authors note the difference was relatively small [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. The Costa Rican eddy-covariance figure is the one directly measured carbon-balance number in the row, but it is a single farm over one study period, not independently replicated, so nothing here reaches the bar for a class [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5]. The evidence spans low/lower-middle-income East African and Indian coffee/coconut systems, pan-tropical cocoa including upper-middle-income Indonesia, and high-income Costa Rican coffee, so even once a class becomes available it would only transfer as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5]. This still does not lift the cell out of data deficiency: it is a single modelled estimate, not independently replicated, it compares two shade densities within the same cocoa system rather than agroforestry against no trees at all, and the authors note the shade contrast is confounded by differences in fertiliser use and hand pollination between the plots they surveyed [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.mechanism: In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii between rows of smallholder coffee and using it as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management because it reduced weeding, with benefit–cost ratios between 3.4 and 5.5 [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry against full-sun cocoa monocultures found that the higher total system production of agroforestry is not reflected in revenues, net present values or production costs: costs did not differ significantly between the systems [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.conditionality: The sources point in different directions for different reasons: the Rwandan saving comes from weed suppression by a mulch-producing legume intercrop, not from shade trees, while the cocoa meta-analysis compares shade-tree agroforestry with full-sun monoculture and finds no significant cost difference [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. Both are crop-specific (coffee and cocoa), from low- and lower-middle-income producing countries, and both concern recurrent production costs (labour, inputs), not establishment costs.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Reviews add that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: In a cocoa plantation in Ghana's Ashanti region, shade trees competed with cocoa for soil water through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought. All cocoa plants under the recommended leguminous shade tree Albizia ferruginea died; cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria, the most common shade tree, suffered 77% mortality and massive stress, with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun; and sap-flux recovery after the drought was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris. Soil water content was higher in full sun than under the shade trees, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: This is a single measured study on a single farm with a few replicate shade trees per species, so the row gives a direction only, with no size class [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The shade-tree species is part of the result: the loss was total under Albizia and heavy under Antiaris, so other shade species, densities or pruning regimes may behave differently. The drought was extreme; the same plots were also measured through wet and normal dry periods, which separates the drought response from ordinary shade effects [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The finding is crop-specific (cocoa) and enters under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; Ghana is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target. A financed shade-cocoa system in a drought-prone area carries this as a risk to the planted asset and the crop.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.mechanism: A review reports, second-hand, that coffee-based agroforestry in Mesoamerica can regulate ecological services including preventing flood occurrences, helping reduce the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: it is a single second-hand review sentence with no effect size, no country or income group, and a general claim about what coffee agroforestry can do rather than a measured flood outcome [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. A further independent source or a measured finding for shaded perennial systems is what is missing.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A coffee review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress (Lin et al. 2008; Meylan et al. 2017), and the IPCC notes, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not say how much that cuts crop losses. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. All are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]; and the review and IPCC statements are second-hand readings of earlier studies [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade trees in coffee and cocoa systems cool the canopy microclimate. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture, with potential to reduce the impact of rising mean temperatures and temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. In Ghana, shade trees were confirmed to moderate the microclimate especially during dry and extremely dry periods, though daily mean maximum air temperatures still reached up to 44°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. In Costa Rica, shade reduces the maximum air temperature by 1.7°C and buffers air and soil temperature, reduces wind speed, and raises relative humidity and soil moisture under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A review synthesis states shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4°C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and in Central America shade trees are reported to have improved microclimate stability [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. Across a multi-country tropical review, trees under canopies averaging 20 m tall gave a temperature reduction of about 2°C compared with a treeless site [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. In Mexican coffee along a shade gradient, the high-shade site fluctuated least around the crop's optimum temperature of 20°C, staying closer to it than medium- and low-shade sites [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter states shade trees can ameliorate increasing stand temperatures that would significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured air temperature 1.3 °C and 1.2 °C cooler and soil-surface temperature 2.1 °C and 2.0 °C cooler than a 15-year-old monoculture, attributed to the alley crops' greater leaf area and ground cover intercepting radiation and reducing vertical mixing of warm air; against both the seven- and 15-year monocultures, the pepper and cacao alleys still measured significantly cooler soil-surface temperatures [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]. In Brazilian coffee, shaded plots measured consistently lower soil temperature at 10 cm depth than unshaded plots, and air temperature under shade had less day-to-day variation and a lower maximum than in the unshaded area [ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_decarvalho21_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The same IPCC chapter immediately adds that the opposite can also be true, pointing to the drought-season soil-water competition recorded in the Ghanaian cocoa study above [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. The same Patil review that found shade stabilising microclimate in Central America also reports that excessive shading combined with heavy rain raised the risk of fungal infection in parts of East Africa [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. For seasonal mean temperature rather than day-to-day fluctuation, the Mexican coffee sites were not significantly different along the shade gradient, which the author reads as shade changing fluctuations more than seasonal means [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. None of the ten units states a size for the gain beyond temperature differences of 1.7 to 4°C; none measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot days or dry seasons [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]. The evidence spans lower-middle, upper-middle, mostly-upper-middle and high-income cocoa and coffee countries across West and Central Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, so it transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. Against the cooling pattern, air temperature in the Malaysian pepper and cacao alleys did not differ from the age-matched seven-year-old monoculture, so the cooling shows up only against the older 15-year stand [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_2]; and bamboo and bactris alleys at the same site measured significantly hotter air (36.4 °C and 37.0 °C) than every other treatment, including both monocultures — a measured harm from the wrong alley crop, which the authors attribute to bamboo's sparse canopy, gaps and low ground cover leaving the soil exposed, concluding bamboo and bactris may not be appropriate intercrops for this reason [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. Both sources are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.mechanism: In shaded coffee and cocoa systems, moderate shade levels can match or slightly exceed full-sun yield while raising the whole system's output. In Costa Rica, moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to or 3% higher than full-sun coffee, and no significant yield difference was found between lightly shaded (<30% cover) and full-sun coffee, with management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. In Rwanda, a Tephrosia vogelii intercrop recycled as mulch in coffee raised parchment yield 23 to 36% over the farmer's own mulch practice across two seasons, though the gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1, ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found total system yield (cocoa plus all by-crops) about ten times higher in agroforestry than monoculture, even though cocoa-bean yield alone was lower [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. In Bolivia, total cocoa-system production was three times higher in agroforestry than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]. A coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss relative to conventional coffee (odds ratio 0.69) and a moderate standardised mean difference favouring agroforestry across yield, bean size and quality outcomes [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]. Shade trees are also reported to reduce the biennial (boom-bust) oscillation of coffee yields, and lower yield variability under more diverse shade is read as greater resistance to shocks [ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. Nitrogen-fixing shade trees (Erythrina poeppigiana, Inga edulis) fix around 100 kg N/ha in coffee systems, ranging 56 to 555 kg/ha across studies [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12]. In Ethiopia, leguminous shade trees at high canopy openness strongly raised coffee yield in El Niño climate-shock years, and leguminous shade with low canopy openness also raised yield across all years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]. In Ghana, whole-farm dry cocoa bean yield was positively associated with upper-canopy shade-tree cover in a model controlling for district, farm size and prior management [ev_crop_yield_asare18_1]. In Ghana, cocoa yield was 13% higher under moderate-shade hybrid cocoa than under full-sun hybrid cocoa [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.conditionality: Against this, the benefit is a dose-response trade-off that turns negative above moderate shade: a coffee meta-analysis found yields declined above 60% shade, with 30 to 60% judged optimal [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3], and in a separate Costa Rican measurement, potential fruit production per coffee bush was 41% lower under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade than under at most 20% cover [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]. The same ten-country cocoa meta-analysis that found a ten-fold total-system gain also found cocoa-bean yield alone 25% lower in agroforestry than full-sun monoculture [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1], a coffee/cocoa review found dry-bean yield per hectare 26% lower under shade than conventional [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1], in Bolivia cocoa productivity (bean yield) was 41% higher in monocultures than agroforestry even though total system production favoured agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6], in Costa Rica coffee yield was 30% lower in agroforestry than monoculture once shade trees established [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11], and in Nicaragua Organic-certified shade coffee showed lower productivity than non-certified [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1.5 t/ha were only possible below 100-150 t C/ha of carbon storage, a direct yield-carbon trade-off [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6]. Several units found no significant yield effect either way: fruiting-node counts in 4-year-old shaded versus full-sun Costa Rican coffee, the shade-by-drought interaction on Ghanaian cocoa yield (shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline), drought yield loss against shade cover across Brazilian cocoa farms, coffee harvest loss against vegetation management in Mexico (all farms lost 18 to 40% regardless of shade complexity), coconut yield with interplanted trees in Kerala except where trees directly shade the palms, and galangal rhizome yield with or without over-canopy [ev_crop_yield_villa20_2, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3]. Tree-cacao water competition under drought is separately reported to reduce soil moisture and push cacao yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. A meta-regression found shade density, region, species and year did not significantly explain the variance in effect size across the pooled coffee studies, meaning the pooled average masks considerable site-to-site variation [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]; soil nitrogen in the cocoa meta-analysis also did not differ significantly between agroforestry and monoculture, so the production gains there do not trace to measured soil fertility [ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1]. The clearest numeric losses (coffee, cocoa) come from Costa Rica, Bolivia, Ghana and a ten-country pool spanning lower-middle to high income; this cell is crop-specific to coffee and cocoa because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. This modelled estimate is confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the shade-density clusters the authors surveyed, and under optimal management the best full-sun clusters reached yields similar to the shaded ones, so the shade share of the gain is uncertain; it adds to the gain side of this row's existing split rather than resolving it [ev_crop_yield_hawkins24_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.mechanism: Returns to farmers, used here as a proxy for rural poverty, tend to be higher in shaded coffee and cocoa. A meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems, with a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. Shade also cushions price shocks: in a case cited second-hand, a coffee price crash cut the net revenue of sun-grown coffee far more (30-fold) than of extensive agroforestry (2.9-fold) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found losses under a 50% coffee price fall were lower for high-shade and diversified systems, with high-shade low-investment farms holding a long-run net present value above zero where low-shade farms averaged one below zero [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2, ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was, by a cited study, almost twice as high in agroforestry as in monoculture, and in Paraná, Brazil a financial model found net present value and benefit-cost index always higher for shaded coffee [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1]. Among certified coffee farms in Nicaragua, C.A.F.E. Practices certification was associated with higher net income [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii grown as mulch within smallholder coffee gave the largest gross margins and returns to labour and the most favourable benefit-cost ratio (5.5) in the first season, from higher coffee yield and less weeding labour [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. In Ghana, moderate-shade hybrid cocoa had by far the highest average plot profitability, with value of production 65% higher than under full-sun hybrid cocoa [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: in a farm survey in Guayas, Ecuador, technified monoculture earned the best net margin per hectare ($2323) against $1565 for organic and $484 for traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2]. Other units find no difference: a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]. What separates the sides is the comparison: the gains are against sun-grown or low-shade systems and under price shocks, while the losses are against an input-intensive technified monoculture. The certification result is bundled, crediting a certification scheme rather than shade alone [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1], the price-fall and net-present-value comparisons are modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1], and the Bolivian labour-return figure is read second-hand [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. The Rwandan result is from the first, unfertilised season of an on-farm trial, and Tephrosia there is a cut-back mulch shrub rather than a shade tree [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the Bolivian one, and the evidence mostly comes from upper-middle- and lower-middle-income producing countries, with low-income Rwanda the exception; returns are proxies for poverty, not poverty itself. This modelled estimate carries wide, overlapping confidence intervals between the shade groups and is confounded by uneven fertiliser use and hand pollination across the surveyed plots, so it reinforces rather than strengthens the row's existing gain side [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.conditionality: This is the shaded perennial-crop family's own row; cocoa and coffee are this family's crops, so the same three units apply directly. Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and both sources are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: The row rests on one study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, which compared farms of differing vegetation management. It found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. For the farmer's harvest, shade trees made no measured difference.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: This is a no-mitigation result from the primary study. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, that more diverse coffee systems suffered less hurricane damage, was dropped from the evidence because the primary does not support it: the difference the study found was in landslides, not in the harvest. The 18 to 40% range is the loss across all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The unit is crop-specific (coffee) and counts because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it is a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and does not state the hurricane's severity [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: One study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Chiapas, Mexico, compared farms of differing vegetation management and found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms losing between 18 and 40% of harvest [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Shade trees did not reduce the hurricane's toll on the coffee harvest in that study.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: The row rests on the primary study's null result, so no mitigation of hurricane harvest loss in shaded coffee is established. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, reporting less damage in more diverse coffee systems, was dropped because the primary does not support it. The 18 to 40% range is the loss on all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The evidence is coffee-specific, counted under the ruling that shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, from a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In a severe drought, the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent across surveyed farms in a Colombian payment-for-ecosystem-services programme [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The loss is in the establishment phase: the source notes established systems were more resilient to drought than traditional pastures [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review, citing Vosti et al. (1998), states that accidental fire is a constant concern for silvopastoral producers because of the damage it could cause to trees and crops, and that post-fire re-establishment costs could be quite high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a second-hand comment on producer concern, not a measured loss, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In Brazil, a review of barriers to silvopastoral adoption notes that in the establishment phase, tree seedlings need protection from excess solar radiation and wind, alongside trampling, herbivory, weed competition and accidental fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. In a US silvopasture trial, heavy thinning of an even-aged stand to open the canopy for forage added extra risk of wind blowdown to the retained trees, with tree productivity in silvopasture described as at potential risk to this kind of damage, though the degree of risk and how management might mitigate it remains understudied [ev_climate_shock_orefice16_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: Both units agree that silvopastoral trees are vulnerable to wind, which is why agreement reads as high despite there being only two units: the Brazilian unit lists wind among several establishment-phase vulnerabilities alongside trampling, herbivory, weeds and fire rather than measuring wind damage itself, and the US unit is an author assertion about risk, not an observed blowdown event. Brazil is upper-middle income and the USA high income, so this scope row sits outside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.mechanism: In Colombian silvopastoral systems, biodiversity rises relative to open pasture, the land use the practice replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Invertebrate abundance showed the largest taxon-specific gain against open pasture, 53.7% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Colombia specifically, a World Bank project evaluation reports that silvopastoral systems played a major role in increasing and conserving biodiversity at farm and landscape level, raising the number of species (richness) and individuals observed (abundance), including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; bird monitoring on Colombian cattle farms found intensive silvopasture had four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A tropical-agroforestry review states that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.conditionality: The same global meta-analysis measures silvopasture against a second, different benchmark — ungrazed native forest — and there the sign reverses: native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower overall biodiversity, 14.8% lower plant biodiversity and 24.4% lower invertebrate biodiversity than native forest, with invertebrate abundance 30.2% lower [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_9, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_11]. This is a conservation benchmark, not the intervention counterfactual: it means silvopasture holds less biodiversity than intact forest, not that converting grazing land to silvopasture reduces biodiversity, so the class is set from the open-pasture comparisons and these forest-benchmark units are held out of it. Two further forest-benchmark comparisons, for birds and bird species richness, found no significant difference, and the invertebrate-abundance gain against open pasture was itself not significant despite a large point estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The meta-analysis does not report the countries behind its figures, so only the Colombian project evidence anchors this row to the LIC/LMIC target; as a pooled global figure it transfers only as adjacent [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The bird-diversity review's single worked example compares recently abandoned pasture against actively grazed pasture, so grazing cessation is confounded with the trees themselves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. These two new dung-beetle units read as a benefit and are weighted heavily enough, alongside the existing Colombian evidence, to move this row's own class from a moderate to a strong gain; they do not touch the separate forest-benchmark comparisons already held out of the class above.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. All of this is global meta-analysis evidence without a Colombia/Costa Rica-specific breakdown, so only the World Bank project and Costa Rican figures anchor the row to its stated countries; as pooled global findings the SOC units transfer only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. Two further readings from the same Colombian Amazon chronosequence measure silvopasture's shallow surface-layer soil carbon against standing native forest rather than against the pasture it replaced, with the traditional pasture on the same land showing a comparable or larger gain over forest in that layer; the engine holds these out of the class for the same reason as the earlier forest-benchmark comparisons in this row — they measure recovery toward a forest reference, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual, and here the gain mostly reflects grass-root carbon inputs after conversion rather than the trees [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_4]. The full-profile null and the unstated-size deeper-layer gain both count toward the same-direction pool without stating a size, which is why only a minority of the same-direction units in this row state how big the effect is, holding the class at moderate; the system is also bundled with tillage, lime and phosphate-rock application at establishment, so the gain cannot be credited to the trees alone. The Brazilian pasture finding is a narrative review citing an underlying primary study without giving its own carbon value or stating the study's duration, so it corroborates the direction of the SOC gain without adding a size [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__catchment_w.mechanism: In a New Zealand silvopasture trial, winter moisture available to recharge the soil profile was lower under silvopasture than under open pasture (113 against 142 mm in a normal-rainfall winter), which the authors attribute to the evergreen pine canopy intercepting rain and continuing to transpire through winter, so silvopasture water use stays higher than open pasture even in the cool season [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1]. After a wetter-than-usual winter, deep drainage below 2 m was detected only under open ryegrass/clover pasture, not under the silvopastures, which the authors read as the silvopastoral trees retaining and using most of the incoming rainfall except in exceptionally wet winters [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__catchment_w.conditionality: Both readings come from one silvopasture experiment in the Canterbury Plains of New Zealand, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target, so the row transfers as out of context. Neither unit measures water leaving the catchment or reaching downstream users; both describe soil-profile recharge and drainage as components of catchment water yield. With only one independent source behind both readings, agreement here is read as low.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_per_he.mechanism: In a US silvopasture establishment trial (forest converted to silvopasture in the Adirondack region of New York), the initial timber-harvesting cost to thin and clear the stand was $1,059 per hectare, which the authors attribute to equipment trucking for a small harvest area, small-diameter stems and research timing [ev_project_cost_orefice16_1]. Forage seeding (orchardgrass and white clover) cost a further $167.04 per hectare, and fencing and water infrastructure $185.33 per hectare, incurred at establishment and again at a mid-rotation replacement [ev_project_cost_orefice16_2, ev_project_cost_orefice16_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_per_he.conditionality: All three figures are actual costs from a single US research trial, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target, and the timber-harvest cost applied equally to the open-pasture comparator the trial used, so it is not a cost specific to silvopasture. With only one independent source behind all three figures, agreement here is read as low, and the figures cannot be converted or pooled into a single range.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.mechanism: A World Bank completion report for Colombia states that production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, attributing the saving to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower incidence of animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the figure is second-hand, an estimate the report takes from a Bank-commissioned business case rather than a measurement, and there is no other source to pool with [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. A further independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing. It comes from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and is a recurrent production-cost saving, not an establishment cost [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk production for agro-pastoralists during drought in a cited Zambian study [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.conditionality: The Zambian unit is a review citing a single study, and the US unit is a background statement used as a soil-water component proxy for drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The US unit is high-income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; only the Zambian unit (low income) is from the target context [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.mechanism: In silvopastoral systems, the benefit runs through fodder availability and herd condition during drought. In Zambia, trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production for agro-pastoralists during drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. In Brazil's semi-arid region, agroforestry biomass productivity varied less over four years than conventional systems, attributed to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.conditionality: Against this, the same Argentine study found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites: at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — the authors attribute the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.mechanism: Silvopasture has been compared with forest and other unmanaged vegetation, not with open pasture. In Washington State, USA, silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth against non-grazed managed forest, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. Across six European Mediterranean countries, an overlay of burnt areas on land use found that, corrected for land-use extent, shrublands carried a greater share of fires than forest, grassland and agroforestry: agroforestry occupied 12% of the area and was associated with 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40% [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Agroforestry's lower share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2], and without the area correction the average fire incidents were lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class; the cell is data deficient. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]; the Mediterranean study compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. The nearest thing to the right comparator is grassland, and there the Mediterranean study found no significant difference, with grassland showing the lowest raw fire incidence [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: trees add woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces, and the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would then point to added risk [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. In the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. The Mediterranean overlay is observational and the agroforestry it maps is existing dehesa- and montado-type grazed wood-pasture, not new planting [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Both studies are from high-income settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.conditionality: Both figures come from a single World Bank project report comparing silvopasture with degraded pasture rather than conventional pasture, and they measure erosion, a component of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.mechanism: Integrated agrosilvopastoral extension may improve diets: a systematic review cites a Kenyan study in which receiving Vi Agroforestry advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of the 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.conditionality: This cell is data deficient, not evidence of no effect. It rests on a single study reported second-hand in a review, from West Pokot, Kenya, and on extension advice rather than silvopasture measured on the farm [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. A second independent source, or the original study's own measurement, would let this cell state a class.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the shade-associated milk and weight-gain figures are associations rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
